  "what happens when a base reacts with a metal": "Some metals such as zinc react with NaOH to give sodium zincate and hydrogen gas.",
  "how do you test for carbon dioxide": "Pass the gas through lime water; it turns milky.",
  "why does hcl gas not change the colour of dry litmus paper": "Acids show their properties only when H⁺ ions are released in the presence of water.",
  "why do acids conduct electricity only in solution": "In water acids produce free ions, which carry current.",
  "why should water not be added to concentrated acid": "Dissolving acid in water is highly exothermic, so water added to acid can splash out. Always add acid slowly to water.",
  "what is the acid in lemon": "Citric acid.",
  "what is the acid in vinegar": "Acetic acid (ethanoic acid).",
  "what is the acid in tamarind": "Tartaric acid.",
  "what is the acid in curd": "Lactic acid.",
  "what is the acid in tomato": "Oxalic acid.",
  "what is the acid in nettle sting": "Methanoic (formic) acid. Rubbing baking soda gives relief.",
  "what is common salt used for": "Common salt (NaCl) is used in food and as the raw material for sodium hydroxide, baking soda, washing soda, bleaching powder and chlorine.",
  "what is the chlor alkali process": "Electrolysis of brine (NaCl solution) gives NaOH at the cathode region, Cl₂ at the anode and H₂ at the cathode.",
  "what is bleaching powder": "Calcium oxychloride, CaOCl₂, made by passing chlorine over dry slaked lime.",
  "what are the uses of bleaching powder": "Bleaching cotton and linen, disinfecting drinking water, and as an oxidising agent in industry.",
  "what is baking soda": "Sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO₃. It is a mild non-corrosive base.",
  "how is baking soda prepared": "NaCl + H₂O + CO₂ + NH₃ → NH₄Cl + NaHCO₃.",
  "what are the uses of baking soda": "In baking powder, antacids, and soda-acid fire extinguishers.",
  "what happens when baking soda is heated": "2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂.",
  "what is baking powder": "A mixture of baking soda and a mild edible acid such as tartaric acid; it makes cakes soft and spongy by releasing CO₂.",
  "what is washing soda": "Sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, obtained by heating baking soda and recrystallising.",
  "what are the uses of washing soda": "Glass, soap and paper industries, removing permanent hardness of water, and as a cleaning agent.",
  "what is water of crystallisation": "The fixed number of water molecules present in one formula unit of a salt, for example 5H₂O in CuSO₄·5H₂O.",
  "what is the colour of copper sulphate crystals": "Blue when hydrated; white when anhydrous.",
  "what is plaster of paris": "Calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO₄·½H₂O, made by heating gypsum at 373 K.",
  "what are the uses of plaster of paris": "Setting fractured bones, making toys, decorative materials and smoothing surfaces.",
  "what is gypsum": "Gypsum is CaSO₄·2H₂O, the raw material for plaster of Paris.",
  "why should plaster of paris be stored in a moisture proof container": "It absorbs moisture and sets into a hard mass of gypsum.",
  "what is neutralisation in daily life": "Using toothpaste (basic) for tooth acid, antacid for indigestion, and baking soda for ant or bee stings.",
  "what is dilution": "Dilution is mixing acid or base with water, which reduces the concentration of ions per unit volume."
},

"3. Metals and Non-metals": {
  "what are the physical properties of metals": "Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile, hard, good conductors of heat and electricity, sonorous, and usually have high melting points.",
  "what are the physical properties of non-metals": "Non-metals are non-lustrous (except iodine), brittle, non-ductile, non-sonorous and poor conductors (except graphite).",
  "what is malleability": "The property of metals to be beaten into thin sheets. Gold and silver are the most malleable.",
  "what is ductility": "The property of metals to be drawn into wires. Gold is the most ductile metal.",
  "what is lustre": "The shiny surface of freshly cut metals.",
  "what is sonorous": "A material that produces a ringing sound when struck.",
  "which metal is liquid at room temperature": "Mercury. Gallium and caesium melt just above room temperature.",
  "which non-metal is liquid at room temperature": "Bromine.",
  "which non-metal conducts electricity": "Graphite, an allotrope of carbon.",
  "which is the hardest natural substance": "Diamond, an allotrope of carbon.",
  "which non-metal is lustrous": "Iodine.",
  "which metals are soft enough to cut with a knife": "Lithium, sodium and potassium.",
  "which metals are the best conductors of heat": "Silver and copper. Lead and mercury are poor conductors.",
  "what is the reactivity series": "A list of metals in decreasing order of reactivity: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Hg, Ag, Au.",
  "why are sodium and potassium kept in kerosene": "They react vigorously with oxygen and moisture and can catch fire, so they are stored under kerosene.",
  "what happens when metals react with oxygen": "Metal oxides are formed, which are generally basic. Example: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO.",
  "what are amphoteric oxides": "Oxides that react with both acids and bases to give salt and water. Examples: Al₂O₃ and ZnO.",
  "what happens when metals react with water": "Active metals give metal hydroxide and hydrogen; less active metals react with steam to give metal oxide and hydrogen.",
  "which metals do not react with water": "Lead, copper, silver and gold do not react with water.",
  "what is aqua regia": "A 3:1 mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated nitric acid; it can dissolve gold and platinum.",
  "what is an ionic compound": "A compound formed by transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal, held by electrostatic force. Example: NaCl.",
  "what are the properties of ionic compounds": "Hard solids, high melting and boiling points, soluble in water, and conduct electricity in molten state or solution.",
  "why do ionic compounds conduct electricity in molten state": "The ions become free to move and carry current.",
  "what is a mineral": "A natural substance in the Earth's crust containing metals or their compounds.",
  "what is an ore": "A mineral from which a metal can be profitably extracted.",
  "what is gangue": "The impurities such as soil and sand present in an ore.",
  "what is metallurgy": "The process of extracting metals from their ores and refining them for use.",
  "what are the steps in extraction of metals": "Enrichment of ore, extracting the metal (reduction), and refining the metal.",
  "what is roasting": "Heating a sulphide ore strongly in excess air to convert it into an oxide. Example: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂.",
  "what is calcination": "Heating a carbonate ore strongly in limited air to convert it into an oxide. Example: ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂.",
  "how are metals in the middle of the reactivity series extracted": "By converting the ore to an oxide (roasting or calcination) and then reducing the oxide with carbon.",
  "how are highly reactive metals extracted": "By electrolysis of their molten chlorides. Example: sodium from molten NaCl.",
  "how is aluminium extracted": "By electrolysis of molten alumina (Al₂O₃) mixed with cryolite; aluminium collects at the cathode.",
  "what is the thermit reaction": "Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → 2Fe + Al₂O₃ + heat; used to join railway tracks and cracked machine parts.",
  "how are metals refined": "Most commonly by electrolytic refining: impure metal is the anode, pure metal is the cathode, and a salt solution is the electrolyte.",
  "what is corrosion of metals": "Slow destruction of metals by air and moisture; iron rusts, copper turns green and silver turns black.",
  "what conditions are needed for rusting": "Both oxygen (air) and water (moisture).",
  "what is an alloy": "A homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal.",
  "what is brass": "An alloy of copper and zinc.",
  "what is bronze": "An alloy of copper and tin.",
  "what is solder": "An alloy of lead and tin with a low melting point, used for welding electrical wires.",
  "what is stainless steel": "An alloy of iron with nickel and chromium that does not rust.",
  "what is an amalgam": "An alloy in which one of the metals is mercury.",
  "why are alloys used": "Alloys are stronger, harder and more resistant to corrosion than pure metals.",
  "why is pure gold alloyed with copper or silver": "Pure gold (24 carat) is too soft for jewellery, so it is alloyed to make it harder.",
  "what is anodising": "Forming a thick protective oxide layer on aluminium by making it the anode in electrolysis.",
  "why does aluminium not corrode easily": "It forms a thin, tough oxide layer on its surface that protects the metal underneath.",
  "do metal oxides and non-metal oxides differ in nature": "Metal oxides are basic; non-metal oxides are acidic.",
  "what is the electronic configuration of sodium": "2, 8, 1. It loses one electron to form Na⁺.",
  "what is the cathode and anode in electrolysis": "Cathode is the negative electrode where reduction occurs; anode is the positive electrode where oxidation occurs."
},

"4. Carbon Compounds": {
  "why does carbon form covalent bonds": "Carbon has four valence electrons and cannot easily lose or gain four electrons, so it shares electrons to form covalent bonds.",
  "what is a covalent bond": "A bond formed by sharing of electrons between two atoms.",
  "what are the properties of covalent compounds": "Low melting and boiling points, poor conductors of electricity, and usually soluble in organic solvents.",
  "what is versatile nature of carbon": "Carbon forms a huge number of compounds due to catenation and tetravalency.",
  "what is catenation": "The ability of carbon atoms to link with each other to form long chains, branched chains and rings.",
  "what is tetravalency": "Carbon has valency four, so it can bond with four other atoms.",
  "what are allotropes of carbon": "Different physical forms of carbon: diamond, graphite and fullerenes.",
  "what is diamond": "A transparent, very hard allotrope of carbon in which each carbon is bonded to four others in a rigid 3D structure.",
  "what is graphite": "A soft, slippery allotrope of carbon with hexagonal layers; it conducts electricity.",
  "what is fullerene": "A cage-like allotrope of carbon, for example C-60, shaped like a football.",
  "why does graphite conduct electricity": "Each carbon atom has a free electron, since only three of its four valence electrons are used in bonding.",
  "what is a hydrocarbon": "A compound made of only carbon and hydrogen.",
  "what are saturated hydrocarbons": "Hydrocarbons with only single bonds between carbon atoms, called alkanes. General formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.",
  "what are unsaturated hydrocarbons": "Hydrocarbons with double (alkenes, CₙH₂ₙ) or triple (alkynes, CₙH₂ₙ₋₂) bonds.",
  "what is the first four alkanes": "Methane (CH₄), ethane (C₂H₆), propane (C₃H₈) and butane (C₄H₁₀).",
  "what is a homologous series": "A series of compounds with the same functional group and similar chemical properties, in which successive members differ by a CH₂ unit.",
  "what is a functional group": "An atom or group of atoms that decides the chemical properties of an organic compound. Examples: -OH, -CHO, -COOH, -Cl.",
  "what is the functional group of alcohol": "Hydroxyl group (-OH).",
  "what is the functional group of aldehyde": "Aldehyde group (-CHO).",
  "what is the functional group of ketone": "Ketone group (>C=O).",
  "what is the functional group of carboxylic acid": "Carboxyl group (-COOH).",
  "what is isomerism": "Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures are called isomers. Example: butane and isobutane.",
  "how many isomers does butane have": "Two: n-butane and isobutane.",
  "what is nomenclature of carbon compounds": "Naming rules: identify the carbon chain, name the functional group as prefix or suffix, and change the ending (-e) as needed.",
  "what is the molecular formula of ethane": "C₂H₆, with seven covalent bonds.",
  "what is the molecular formula of ethene": "C₂H₄, with a carbon-carbon double bond.",
  "what is the molecular formula of ethyne": "C₂H₂, with a carbon-carbon triple bond.",
  "what is combustion of carbon compounds": "Burning in oxygen to give carbon dioxide, water, heat and light. Example: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.",
  "why do saturated hydrocarbons burn with a blue flame": "They burn completely in sufficient air. Unsaturated hydrocarbons burn with a yellow sooty flame due to incomplete combustion.",
  "what is an oxidation reaction in carbon compounds": "Alcohols can be oxidised to carboxylic acids using alkaline KMnO₄ or acidified potassium dichromate.",
  "what is an addition reaction": "Unsaturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen in presence of nickel or palladium catalyst to become saturated. Used to make vegetable ghee from oil.",
  "what is a substitution reaction": "A reaction in which one atom is replaced by another, for example methane and chlorine in sunlight: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.",
  "what is ethanol": "Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) is a colourless liquid, soluble in water, found in alcoholic drinks.",
  "what are the reactions of ethanol": "With sodium it gives sodium ethoxide and hydrogen; heating with excess conc. H₂SO₄ at 443 K gives ethene.",
  "what is dehydration of ethanol": "Heating ethanol with conc. H₂SO₄ at 443 K removes water and gives ethene.",
  "what is ethanoic acid": "Ethanoic (acetic) acid, CH₃COOH. A 5-8 percent solution in water is vinegar.",
  "what is glacial acetic acid": "Pure ethanoic acid, which freezes into a ice-like solid at 290 K.",
  "what is esterification": "Carboxylic acid reacts with alcohol in presence of acid catalyst to form a sweet-smelling ester and water.",
  "what is saponification": "Hydrolysis of an ester with sodium hydroxide to give alcohol and sodium salt of the carboxylic acid (soap).",
  "what are esters used for": "Making perfumes and flavouring agents.",
  "what is denatured alcohol": "Ethanol made unfit for drinking by adding poisonous substances such as methanol.",
  "what are the harmful effects of drinking alcohol": "Damage to liver and nervous system, impaired judgement and addiction. Methanol is poisonous and can cause blindness.",
  "what is soap": "Sodium or potassium salt of long-chain carboxylic acids used for cleaning.",
  "what is a micelle": "A spherical cluster of soap molecules with hydrocarbon tails inside and ionic ends outside, which traps oil and dirt.",
  "how do soaps clean": "The hydrophobic tail attaches to oil while the hydrophilic head stays in water, forming micelles that carry dirt away.",
  "what is a detergent": "A sodium salt of sulphonic acid or ammonium salt with chloride or bromide ions, used for cleaning.",
  "what is hard water": "Water containing calcium and magnesium salts, which forms scum with soap.",
  "what is the difference between soap and detergent": "Soap forms scum in hard water; detergents do not, because their calcium and magnesium salts are soluble.",
  "what is scum": "The insoluble precipitate formed when soap reacts with calcium or magnesium salts in hard water.",
  "what is the electronic dot structure of methane": "Carbon shares one electron with each of four hydrogen atoms, forming four single covalent bonds.",
  "what is the electron dot structure of oxygen": "Two oxygen atoms share two pairs of electrons, forming a double bond (O=O).",
  "what is the electron dot structure of nitrogen": "Two nitrogen atoms share three pairs of electrons, forming a triple bond (N≡N)."
},

"5. Periodic Classification": {
  "what is dobereiner's triad": "Groups of three elements with similar properties in which the atomic mass of the middle element is the mean of the other two. Example: Li, Na, K.",
  "what is newlands law of octaves": "When elements are arranged by increasing atomic mass, every eighth element has properties similar to the first, like musical notes.",
  "what is mendeleev's periodic law": "The properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses.",
  "what is the modern periodic law": "The properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.",
  "what are the achievements of mendeleev's periodic table": "He left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties, for example eka-aluminium (gallium) and eka-silicon (germanium).",
  "what are the limitations of mendeleev's periodic table": "The position of hydrogen was not fixed, isotopes had no place, and atomic mass did not increase regularly.",
  "how many groups and periods are in the modern periodic table": "18 groups (vertical columns) and 7 periods (horizontal rows).",
  "what are alkali metals": "Group 1 elements: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr. They are very reactive soft metals.",
  "what are alkaline earth metals": "Group 2 elements: Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra.",
  "what are halogens": "Group 17 elements: F, Cl, Br, I, At. They are very reactive non-metals.",
  "what are noble gases": "Group 18 elements: He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn. They have a complete outermost shell and are chemically inert.",
  "what is valency": "The combining capacity of an atom, the number of electrons it loses, gains or shares.",
  "what is atomic size": "The distance from the centre of the nucleus to the outermost shell of an atom.",
  "how does atomic size change in a period": "It decreases from left to right because nuclear charge increases and pulls electrons closer.",
  "how does atomic size change in a group": "It increases down a group because new shells are added.",
  "how does metallic character change in a period": "Metallic character decreases from left to right across a period.",
  "how does metallic character change in a group": "Metallic character increases down a group.",
  "how does valency change in a period": "Valency increases from 1 to 4 and then decreases to 0 across a period.",
  "how does valency change in a group": "Valency remains the same down a group, because the number of valence electrons is the same.",
  "how does electronegativity change in a period": "It increases from left to right across a period.",
  "what is the most reactive metal in the periodic table": "Francium (practically caesium), at the bottom of group 1.",
  "what is the most reactive non-metal": "Fluorine.",
  "why are noble gases inert": "Their outermost shells are completely filled (octet or duplet), so they neither gain, lose nor share electrons.",
  "what are the elements of the second period": "Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, Ne.",
  "what is the position of hydrogen in the periodic table": "Hydrogen is placed above group 1 as it resembles alkali metals (one electron) and halogens (diatomic).",
  "what are metalloids": "Elements with properties of both metals and non-metals, such as silicon and germanium.",
  "what is the number of elements in the first three periods": "The first period has 2 elements, the second 8 and the third 8."
},

"6. Life Processes": {
  "what are life processes": "Processes necessary to maintain life: nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion.",
  "what is nutrition": "Nutrition is the process of obtaining and using food for energy, growth and repair.",
  "what is autotrophic nutrition": "Organisms make their own food from simple inorganic substances such as CO₂ and water. Example: green plants.",
  "what is heterotrophic nutrition": "Organisms depend on other organisms for food. Example: animals and fungi.",
  "what is photosynthesis": "The process by which green plants make carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight and chlorophyll.",
  "what is the equation of photosynthesis": "6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (in presence of sunlight and chlorophyll).",
  "what are the events during photosynthesis": "Absorption of light by chlorophyll, conversion of light energy into chemical energy with splitting of water, and reduction of CO₂ to carbohydrates.",
  "what is chlorophyll": "The green pigment in chloroplasts that traps sunlight for photosynthesis.",
  "what are stomata": "Tiny pores in leaves for gas exchange and transpiration, controlled by guard cells.",
  "what do guard cells do": "They open and close the stomata by swelling or shrinking when water enters or leaves them.",
  "what is holozoic nutrition": "Ingestion of solid food, digestion, absorption and egestion. Example: humans, amoeba.",
  "what is saprophytic nutrition": "Obtaining food from dead and decaying matter. Example: fungi such as bread mould.",
  "what is parasitic nutrition": "Obtaining food from the body of a living host. Examples: Cuscuta, tapeworm, ticks.",
  "how does amoeba take food": "By engulfing it with pseudopodia, forming a food vacuole in which digestion occurs.",
  "what is the human digestive system": "A long tube (alimentary canal) from mouth to anus, with salivary glands, liver and pancreas as accessory glands.",
  "what is the role of saliva": "It moistens food and contains salivary amylase that breaks starch into sugar.",
  "what is peristalsis": "Rhythmic contraction and relaxation of the alimentary canal that pushes food forward.",
  "what is the role of the stomach in digestion": "Gastric glands release hydrochloric acid, pepsin and mucus; pepsin digests proteins.",
  "what is the role of hydrochloric acid in the stomach": "It makes the medium acidic for pepsin to work and kills bacteria in food.",
  "what is the role of mucus in the stomach": "It protects the stomach lining from the acid.",
  "what is the role of bile": "Bile from the liver makes the food alkaline and emulsifies fats into small globules.",
  "what is the role of the pancreas in digestion": "It secretes pancreatic juice containing trypsin (proteins), lipase (fats) and amylase (starch).",
  "what is the role of the small intestine": "Complete digestion and absorption of food. Intestinal juice converts proteins to amino acids, carbohydrates to glucose and fats to fatty acids.",
  "what are villi": "Finger-like projections in the small intestine that increase the surface area for absorption.",
  "what is the role of the large intestine": "It absorbs water; the remaining waste is removed through the anus.",
  "what is respiration": "The process of releasing energy from food in the cells, stored as ATP.",
  "what is aerobic respiration": "Breakdown of glucose using oxygen into CO₂ and water, releasing a large amount of energy (38 ATP).",
  "what is anaerobic respiration": "Breakdown of glucose without oxygen. In yeast it gives ethanol and CO₂; in muscles it gives lactic acid.",
  "what is atp": "Adenosine triphosphate, the energy currency of the cell.",
  "what is glycolysis": "The first step of respiration in the cytoplasm, in which glucose (6C) breaks into pyruvate (3C).",
  "why do muscles cramp after heavy exercise": "Lack of oxygen converts pyruvate to lactic acid, which builds up in the muscles.",
  "what is the difference between breathing and respiration": "Breathing is the physical intake and release of air; respiration is the chemical release of energy from food in cells.",
  "what is the pathway of air in humans": "Nostrils, nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli.",
  "what are alveoli": "Tiny balloon-like sacs in the lungs with a large surface area where gas exchange takes place.",
  "what is haemoglobin": "A red respiratory pigment in red blood cells that carries oxygen; it has high affinity for oxygen.",
  "how does breathing occur": "During inhalation the diaphragm flattens and ribs move up and out; during exhalation the opposite happens.",
  "how do aquatic animals breathe": "Fish use gills to take dissolved oxygen from water. Water contains less oxygen so they breathe faster.",
  "what is transportation in humans": "Blood carries food, oxygen, waste and hormones through blood vessels pumped by the heart.",
  "what are the chambers of the human heart": "Four: two upper atria (receive blood) and two lower ventricles (pump blood).",
  "what is double circulation": "Blood passes through the heart twice in one complete cycle: pulmonary circulation and systemic circulation.",
  "what is the difference between arteries and veins": "Arteries carry blood away from the heart and have thick walls; veins bring blood to the heart, have thin walls and valves.",
  "what are capillaries": "Thin-walled tiny vessels where exchange of materials between blood and cells takes place.",
  "what is blood": "A fluid connective tissue made of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.",
  "what is the function of rbc": "Red blood cells carry oxygen with the help of haemoglobin.",
  "what is the function of wbc": "White blood cells fight infection and disease.",
  "what is the function of platelets": "They help in blood clotting at the site of injury.",
  "what is plasma": "The liquid part of blood that carries food, CO₂ and nitrogenous wastes.",
  "what is blood pressure": "The force of blood against the walls of vessels. Normal is about 120 mm Hg (systolic) over 80 mm Hg (diastolic).",
  "what is a sphygmomanometer": "An instrument that measures blood pressure.",
  "what is lymph": "A colourless fluid like plasma that carries digested fat and drains excess fluid from tissues back into blood.",
  "what is xylem": "Plant tissue that transports water and minerals from roots to other parts.",
  "what is phloem": "Plant tissue that transports food (sugars) from leaves to other parts.",
  "what is transpiration": "Loss of water vapour from aerial parts of the plant, mainly through stomata. It helps absorb and transport water and cools the plant.",
  "what is translocation": "The transport of soluble food made in leaves to other parts of the plant through the phloem.",
  "what is root pressure": "The pressure created by roots that pushes water up the xylem.",
  "what is excretion": "The removal of harmful metabolic wastes from the body.",
  "what are the parts of the human excretory system": "Two kidneys, two ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra.",
  "what is a nephron": "The structural and functional unit of the kidney, made of glomerulus, Bowman's capsule and a long tubule.",
  "how is urine formed": "By filtration of blood in the glomerulus, selective reabsorption of useful substances in the tubule, and secretion of waste.",
  "what is dialysis": "Artificial filtering of blood in an artificial kidney (haemodialysis) for patients whose kidneys have failed.",
  "how do plants get rid of wastes": "Through stomata, falling leaves, bark, gums and resins, and by storing wastes in cell vacuoles."
},

"7. Control and Coordination": {
  "what is control and coordination": "Working together of the nervous system and hormones so that body parts respond properly to stimuli.",
  "what is a stimulus": "A change in the environment that an organism responds to.",
  "what is a receptor": "A sensory structure that detects a stimulus. Examples: eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin.",
  "what is a neuron": "The structural and functional unit of the nervous system, made of dendrites, a cell body and an axon.",
  "what is a dendrite": "The part of a neuron that receives information.",
  "what is an axon": "The long part of a neuron that carries impulses away from the cell body.",
  "what is a synapse": "The gap between two neurons where an electrical impulse is converted into a chemical signal and passed on.",
  "what is a reflex action": "A sudden, automatic response to a stimulus without thinking. Example: pulling the hand away from a hot object.",
  "what is a reflex arc": "The pathway of a reflex: receptor, sensory neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron and effector.",
  "why are reflex arcs formed": "Thinking takes time, so reflex arcs give a quick response for protection.",
  "what are the parts of the human brain": "Forebrain (cerebrum), midbrain and hindbrain (cerebellum, pons and medulla).",
  "what is the function of the cerebrum": "Thinking, memory, voluntary actions, hearing, smell, sight and hunger.",
  "what is the function of the cerebellum": "Maintains posture and balance and coordinates voluntary movements.",
  "what is the function of the medulla": "Controls involuntary actions such as blood pressure, salivation and vomiting.",
  "what is the spinal cord": "A cylinder of nerve tissue from the brain that carries messages and controls reflex actions.",
  "how is the brain protected": "By the skull (cranium) and a fluid-filled balloon called cerebrospinal fluid.",
  "what is the difference between voluntary and involuntary actions": "Voluntary actions are controlled by the forebrain; involuntary actions are controlled by the medulla.",
  "what is a muscle response": "Animal cells change shape using special proteins that move in response to a nerve impulse.",
  "what is a plant hormone": "A chemical produced in plants that coordinates growth and responses.",
  "what is auxin": "A plant hormone that promotes cell elongation. It is made at the tip of shoots.",
  "what is gibberellin": "A plant hormone that helps in stem growth.",
  "what is cytokinin": "A plant hormone that promotes cell division, abundant in fruits and seeds.",
  "what is abscisic acid": "A plant hormone that inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves.",
  "what is ethylene": "A gaseous plant hormone that ripens fruits.",
  "what is tropism": "Directional growth movement of a plant in response to a stimulus.",
  "what is phototropism": "Movement in response to light. Shoots bend towards light and roots bend away.",
  "what is geotropism": "Movement in response to gravity. Roots grow downward and shoots grow upward.",
  "what is hydrotropism": "Movement of roots towards water.",
  "what is chemotropism": "Growth in response to chemicals, such as pollen tube growing towards the ovule.",
  "what is thigmotropism": "Growth in response to touch, such as tendrils coiling around a support.",
  "what is a nastic movement": "A non-directional response to a stimulus, such as the drooping of leaves of the touch-me-not plant.",
  "why do the leaves of touch me not plant droop": "Water leaves the cells quickly on touch, so the cells shrink and the leaves fold.",
  "what is a hormone": "A chemical secreted by endocrine glands directly into the blood that controls and coordinates body functions.",
  "what is an endocrine gland": "A ductless gland that secretes hormones into the blood.",
  "what is the master gland": "The pituitary gland, as it controls the activity of other endocrine glands.",
  "what is the function of growth hormone": "It regulates growth and development. Too little causes dwarfism; too much causes gigantism.",
  "what is thyroxine": "A hormone from the thyroid gland that regulates carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism; it needs iodine.",
  "what is goitre": "Swelling of the neck due to lack of iodine in the diet, which reduces thyroxine production.",
  "why is iodised salt recommended": "Iodine is needed to make thyroxine and prevents goitre.",
  "what is insulin": "A hormone from the pancreas that lowers blood sugar. Deficiency causes diabetes.",
  "what is adrenaline": "A hormone from the adrenal glands that prepares the body for fight or flight by raising heart rate and breathing.",
  "what is testosterone": "The male sex hormone from the testes, responsible for male features at puberty.",
  "what is oestrogen": "The female sex hormone from the ovaries, responsible for female features at puberty.",
  "what is the feedback mechanism": "A system that regulates hormone release; when the blood sugar level rises the pancreas makes more insulin, and when it falls insulin secretion drops."
},

"8. How Organisms Reproduce": {
  "what is reproduction": "The process by which organisms produce new individuals of their own kind.",
  "why is dna copying important in reproduction": "It passes on the body design and traits to the next generation and also creates small variations.",
  "why is variation important": "It helps species survive environmental changes and drives evolution.",
  "what is asexual reproduction": "Reproduction by a single parent without gametes, giving genetically identical offspring.",
  "what is binary fission": "A cell divides into two equal halves. Example: amoeba, bacteria.",
  "what is multiple fission": "A cell divides into many daughter cells at once. Example: Plasmodium.",
  "what is fragmentation": "An organism breaks into pieces and each grows into a new individual. Example: Spirogyra.",
  "what is regeneration": "Growing new individuals from body parts of a broken organism. Example: Hydra and Planaria.",
  "what is budding": "A bud develops as an outgrowth and detaches to become a new individual. Example: Hydra and yeast.",
  "what is vegetative propagation": "New plants arise from vegetative parts such as the root, stem or leaf. Example: potato, Bryophyllum, rose.",
  "what are the advantages of vegetative propagation": "Plants bear flowers and fruits earlier and are genetically similar to the parent; seedless plants like banana and jasmine can be grown.",
  "what are layering and grafting": "Methods of vegetative propagation. In layering a branch is bent into soil to root; in grafting the cutting of one plant is joined to another.",
  "what is tissue culture": "Growing new plants from a few cells of a plant in a nutrient medium under sterile conditions.",
  "what is spore formation": "Tiny reproductive spores in a sporangium burst and grow into new individuals. Example: Rhizopus.",
  "what is sexual reproduction": "Reproduction involving two parents and the fusion of male and female gametes.",
  "what are the advantages of sexual reproduction": "It produces variation, which helps species survive and evolve.",
  "what are the parts of a flower": "Sepals, petals, stamens (male) and pistil/carpel (female).",
  "what is the stamen": "The male part of the flower made of anther and filament; the anther produces pollen.",
  "what is the pistil": "The female part of the flower consisting of stigma, style and ovary.",
  "what is pollination": "Transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma.",
  "what is self pollination": "Transfer of pollen to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant.",
  "what is cross pollination": "Transfer of pollen from one flower to the stigma of a flower on another plant.",
  "what is fertilisation": "Fusion of the male gamete with the female gamete to form a zygote.",
  "what happens after fertilisation in plants": "The zygote becomes an embryo, the ovule becomes the seed, the ovary becomes the fruit and other floral parts wither.",
  "what is a pollen tube": "A tube that grows from the pollen grain through the style carrying male gametes to the ovule.",
  "what is germination": "The growth of a seed into a seedling under suitable conditions.",
  "what is the male reproductive system": "It includes testes, scrotum, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate gland and penis.",
  "why are testes in the scrotum": "Sperm formation needs a temperature lower than body temperature.",
  "what is the function of the testes": "They produce sperm and the hormone testosterone.",
  "what is the female reproductive system": "It includes ovaries, oviducts (fallopian tubes), uterus and vagina.",
  "what is the function of the ovary": "It produces eggs and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone.",
  "where does fertilisation occur in humans": "In the oviduct (fallopian tube).",
  "what is the zygote": "The cell formed by the fusion of sperm and egg.",
  "what is implantation": "The attachment of the embryo to the lining of the uterus.",
  "what is the placenta": "A disc-like tissue that supplies nutrition and oxygen from the mother to the embryo and removes wastes.",
  "what is menstruation": "The breakdown and discharge of the uterine lining along with blood when the egg is not fertilised, about every 28 days.",
  "what is puberty": "The age when sex hormones become active and sexual maturity develops.",
  "what is menopause": "The end of menstrual cycles in women at about 45-50 years of age.",
  "what are contraceptive methods": "Barrier methods (condoms), chemical methods (oral pills), IUDs (Copper-T) and surgical methods (vasectomy and tubectomy).",
  "what is vasectomy": "A surgical method of birth control in which the vas deferens is blocked or cut in males.",
  "what is tubectomy": "A surgical method of birth control in which the fallopian tubes are blocked in females.",
  "what are sexually transmitted diseases": "Diseases spread by sexual contact such as gonorrhoea, syphilis, warts and HIV-AIDS. Condoms help prevent them.",
  "what is aids": "Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome caused by HIV, which weakens the immune system.",
  "what decides the sex of a child": "The father's chromosome. A sperm with X gives a girl; a sperm with Y gives a boy.",
  "what is female foeticide": "The illegal practice of aborting a female foetus; it is a crime that reduces the sex ratio.",
  "what is the difference between fission and fragmentation": "In fission a unicellular organism divides into two or many; in fragmentation a multicellular organism breaks into pieces that each grow."
},

"9. Heredity and Evolution": {
  "what is heredity": "The transmission of characters from parents to offspring.",
  "what is variation": "Differences between individuals of the same species.",
  "who is the father of genetics": "Gregor Johann Mendel.",
  "what plant did mendel use": "The garden pea (Pisum sativum).",
  "why did mendel choose pea plants": "They have clear contrasting traits, short life cycle, are self-pollinating and produce many seeds.",
  "what is a gene": "A segment of DNA that carries information for a trait.",
  "what is a trait": "A characteristic of an organism, such as height or flower colour.",
  "what is a dominant trait": "A trait that appears in the F1 generation when two contrasting traits are crossed.",
  "what is a recessive trait": "A trait that is hidden in F1 and reappears in F2.",
  "what is genotype": "The genetic makeup of an organism, for example TT or Tt.",
  "what is phenotype": "The visible expression of a trait, for example tall or dwarf.",
  "what is a monohybrid cross": "A cross between two parents that differ in one trait. The F2 phenotypic ratio is 3:1 and the genotypic ratio is 1:2:1.",
  "what is a dihybrid cross": "A cross involving two traits. The F2 phenotypic ratio is 9:3:3:1.",
  "what is mendel's law of independent assortment": "Traits are inherited independently of each other.",
  "what is an allele": "Alternative forms of a gene, such as T and t.",
  "what are acquired traits": "Traits developed during the lifetime of an individual that are not passed to offspring, such as a cut tail.",
  "what are inherited traits": "Traits passed from parents through genes, such as eye colour.",
  "what is the number of chromosomes in humans": "46 chromosomes, or 23 pairs.",
  "what are sex chromosomes": "X and Y chromosomes: females have XX and males have XY.",
  "how is sex determined in humans": "The egg always carries X; the sperm carries X or Y. XX gives a girl and XY gives a boy.",
  "what is evolution": "The gradual change in organisms over generations, leading to new species.",
  "what is speciation": "The formation of new species from existing ones.",
  "what factors lead to speciation": "Geographical isolation, genetic drift, natural selection and variation.",
  "what is natural selection": "The process in which organisms with favourable variations survive and reproduce more. Proposed by Charles Darwin.",
  "what is genetic drift": "Random change in the frequency of genes in a small population.",
  "what is gene flow": "Transfer of genes between populations through migration.",
  "what are fossils": "Preserved remains or impressions of organisms that lived in the past.",
  "how is the age of fossils determined": "By the depth of the rock layer (relative dating) and by radioactive dating such as carbon-14.",
  "what are homologous organs": "Organs with the same basic structure but different functions, such as the forelimbs of a human, bat and whale. They show common ancestry.",
  "what are analogous organs": "Organs with different structures but similar functions, such as wings of a bird and an insect.",
  "what are vestigial organs": "Reduced organs with no function in the present, such as the appendix in humans.",
  "what is archaeopteryx": "A fossil with feathered wings like a bird and teeth and tail like a reptile, showing that birds evolved from reptiles.",
  "what is evolutionary relationship": "The closer two species are, the more recently they shared a common ancestor and the more similar their characters.",
  "where did the human species originate": "In Africa; Homo sapiens spread from there to other continents.",
  "what is the evolution of eyes": "Eyes evolved independently several times, showing that complex organs form in small steps.",
  "what is artificial selection": "Humans selecting organisms with desirable traits to breed, such as the wild cabbage producing cabbage, broccoli and kale.",
  "what is the role of dna in heredity": "DNA carries the genetic information, and its copying passes traits to offspring."
},

"10. Light: Reflection and Refraction": {
  "what is the pole of a mirror": "The centre of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror.",
  "what is the centre of curvature": "The centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part.",
  "what is the radius of curvature": "The radius of the sphere of which the mirror is a part. R = 2f.",
  "what is the principal axis": "The line passing through the pole and the centre of curvature of a spherical mirror.",
  "what is the principal focus of a concave mirror": "The point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis meet after reflection.",
  "what is the aperture of a mirror": "The diameter of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror.",
  "what is the relation between focal length and radius of curvature": "f = R/2.",
  "what are the laws of reflection": "The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane.",
  "what is the image formed by a plane mirror": "Virtual, erect, laterally inverted, same size as the object, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.",
  "what is the new cartesian sign convention": "The pole is the origin; distances along the incident light are positive; distances above the axis are positive; below the axis they are negative.",
  "what is the image formed by a concave mirror when the object is at infinity": "A real, inverted, highly diminished image at the focus.",
  "what is the image formed by a concave mirror when the object is between pole and focus": "A virtual, erect and enlarged image behind the mirror.",
  "what is the image formed by a concave mirror when the object is at the centre of curvature": "A real, inverted image of the same size at the centre of curvature.",
  "what is the image formed by a convex mirror": "Always virtual, erect and diminished, located between the pole and the focus.",
  "what are the uses of a concave mirror": "Shaving mirrors, torches, vehicle headlights, dentists' mirrors and solar furnaces.",
  "what are the uses of a convex mirror": "Rear-view mirrors in vehicles and security mirrors in shops.",
  "why are convex mirrors used as rear view mirrors": "They give an erect, diminished image and a wider field of view.",
  "why do dentists use concave mirrors": "A concave mirror gives a magnified, erect image of the teeth when held close.",
  "what is refraction of light": "The bending of light when it passes from one transparent medium into another due to a change in its speed.",
  "what are the laws of refraction": "The incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in the same plane, and sin i / sin r is constant for a given pair of media (Snell's law).",
  "what is refractive index of a medium": "The ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed of light in that medium, n = c/v.",
  "what is the absolute refractive index of water and glass": "About 1.33 for water and 1.5 for ordinary glass.",
  "what is an optically denser medium": "A medium with a higher refractive index, in which light travels more slowly.",
  "how does light bend when it enters a denser medium": "It bends towards the normal.",
  "how does light bend when it enters a rarer medium": "It bends away from the normal.",
  "what is the principal focus of a convex lens": "The point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet after refraction.",
  "what is the optical centre of a lens": "The central point of a lens; a ray through it passes undeviated.",
  "what is the image formed by a convex lens when the object is beyond 2f": "A real, inverted and diminished image between f and 2f.",
  "what is the image formed by a convex lens when the object is between f and optical centre": "A virtual, erect and enlarged image on the same side as the object (magnifier).",
  "what is the image formed by a concave lens": "Always virtual, erect and diminished, between the optical centre and the focus.",
  "what are the uses of a convex lens": "Magnifying glasses, cameras, microscopes, telescopes and spectacles for hypermetropia.",
  "what are the uses of a concave lens": "Spectacles for myopia, peepholes in doors and some optical instruments.",
  "what is the power of a lens": "The reciprocal of focal length in metres, P = 1/f. The unit is dioptre (D).",
  "what is the sign of power of convex and concave lenses": "Convex lens has positive power; concave lens has negative power.",
  "what is the magnification of a lens": "The ratio of image height to object height, m = h'/h = v/u.",
  "what is the apparent bending of a pencil in water": "It is due to refraction of light as it goes from water to air.",
  "why does a stream bed appear raised": "Due to refraction, light from the bottom bends away from the normal making it appear nearer the surface."
},

"11. The Human Eye and the Colourful World": {
  "what is the human eye": "A natural optical instrument that forms an image of objects on the retina.",
  "what is the cornea": "The transparent front part of the eye where most of the refraction of light occurs.",
  "what is the iris": "The coloured muscular diaphragm that controls the size of the pupil.",
  "what is the pupil": "The opening in the iris through which light enters the eye.",
  "what is the eye lens": "A convex lens that focuses light onto the retina; its focal length is changed by the ciliary muscles.",
  "what are the ciliary muscles": "Muscles that change the curvature of the eye lens for focusing.",
  "what is the retina": "The light-sensitive screen at the back of the eye that forms the image and has rods and cones.",
  "what do rods and cones do": "Rods respond to dim light; cones respond to bright light and colours.",
  "what is the optic nerve": "The nerve that carries signals from the retina to the brain.",
  "what is the blind spot": "The point on the retina where the optic nerve leaves; it has no light-sensitive cells.",
  "what is the power of accommodation of the eye": "The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length to see both near and distant objects.",
  "what is the least distance of distinct vision": "About 25 cm for a young adult.",
  "what is the range of vision of a normal eye": "From 25 cm to infinity.",
  "what is persistence of vision": "The image stays on the retina for about 1/16 second after the object is removed.",
  "what is cataract": "Clouding of the eye lens, causing blurred vision; treated by surgery.",
  "what is myopia and how is it corrected": "Near-sightedness: distant objects look blurred because the image forms in front of the retina. Corrected with a concave lens.",
  "what is hypermetropia and how is it corrected": "Far-sightedness: near objects look blurred because the image forms behind the retina. Corrected with a convex lens.",
  "what is presbyopia and how is it corrected": "Weakening of accommodation with age. Corrected by bifocal lenses.",
  "what causes myopia": "Excessive curvature of the eye lens or elongation of the eyeball.",
  "what causes hypermetropia": "The focal length of the eye lens is too long or the eyeball is too small.",
  "why do we have two eyes": "Two eyes give a wider field of view and allow us to judge depth (three-dimensional vision).",
  "why should eyes be donated": "A donated cornea can restore sight to a person with corneal blindness.",
  "what is a prism": "A transparent triangular solid with two refracting surfaces that bends and disperses light.",
  "what is dispersion of white light": "Splitting of white light into seven colours by a glass prism. Violet bends the most and red the least.",
  "who first discovered the spectrum": "Isaac Newton, with a glass prism.",
  "what is a rainbow": "A natural spectrum formed by dispersion, refraction and internal reflection of sunlight in water droplets, seen when the Sun is behind the observer.",
  "what is atmospheric refraction": "The bending of light by layers of the atmosphere with varying optical density.",
  "why do stars twinkle": "Atmospheric refraction changes the apparent position and brightness of the starlight, since its path keeps varying.",
  "why do planets not twinkle": "Planets are nearer, so they behave as extended sources made of many point sources whose variations average out.",
  "why does the sun appear before actual sunrise": "Atmospheric refraction raises the apparent position of the Sun, so it is seen about 2 minutes early and seen for 2 minutes after sunset.",
  "why does the sun look flattened at sunset": "Atmospheric refraction affects the rays from the top and bottom edges of the Sun differently.",
  "why is the sky blue": "Air molecules scatter shorter wavelengths (blue) more strongly than longer wavelengths (red).",
  "why does the sky look dark in space": "There is no atmosphere in space to scatter sunlight.",
  "why is the sun red at sunrise and sunset": "Sunlight travels a longer path through the atmosphere, so blue is scattered away and red reaches us.",
  "why are danger signals red": "Red light is scattered the least by fog and smoke, so it can be seen from far away.",
  "what is the tyndall effect in daily life": "Seen when a beam of sunlight enters a dusty room or passes through the canopy of a dense forest, as particles scatter light."
},

"12. Electricity": {
  "what is an electric circuit": "A continuous closed path of an electric current.",
  "what is the unit of electric current": "Ampere (A). One ampere is one coulomb of charge flowing per second.",
  "what is the direction of conventional current": "From the positive terminal to the negative terminal; electrons move in the opposite direction.",
  "what is electric potential difference": "The work done to move a unit charge between two points: V = W/Q. The unit is volt.",
  "what is one volt of potential difference": "One volt is when 1 joule of work is done to move 1 coulomb of charge.",
  "what is an ammeter used for": "To measure current. It is connected in series with very low resistance.",
  "what is a voltmeter used for": "To measure potential difference. It is connected in parallel with very high resistance.",
  "what is ohm's law formula": "V = IR; the current is proportional to the potential difference at constant temperature.",
  "what is one ohm": "The resistance of a conductor when a potential difference of 1 V gives a current of 1 A.",
  "what factors does resistance of a conductor depend on": "Length (directly), area of cross-section (inversely), material and temperature.",
  "what is the formula of resistance in terms of resistivity": "R = ρl/A.",
  "what is the unit of resistivity": "Ohm-metre (Ω m).",
  "which materials have the lowest resistivity": "Silver and copper are the best conductors; alloys have higher resistivity than pure metals.",
  "why are alloys used in heating devices": "Alloys have high resistivity and do not oxidise or burn easily at high temperatures.",
  "why is tungsten used in bulb filaments": "It has a very high melting point (3380°C) and high resistivity.",
  "why are bulbs filled with nitrogen or argon": "Inert gas prolongs the life of the filament by preventing oxidation.",
  "what is a rheostat": "A variable resistor used to change the current in a circuit.",
  "what is resistance in series": "R = R₁ + R₂ + R₃; the same current flows through each resistor.",
  "what is resistance in parallel": "1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃; the potential difference is the same across each resistor.",
  "why are household circuits wired in parallel": "Each appliance gets the same voltage and works independently, and total resistance is lower.",
  "what is the heating effect of current": "Electrical energy is converted into heat when current flows in a resistor.",
  "what is joule's law of heating": "H = I²Rt; heat produced is proportional to the square of current, the resistance and time.",
  "what are the applications of the heating effect of current": "Electric heaters, irons, toasters, kettles, bulbs and fuses.",
  "what is a fuse": "A safety device with a wire of low melting point that melts when excess current flows and breaks the circuit.",
  "what is electric power": "The rate of consumption of electric energy: P = VI = I²R = V²/R. The unit is watt.",
  "what is the commercial unit of electric energy": "Kilowatt hour (kWh): 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.",
  "how do you calculate electric energy": "Energy = power × time.",
  "what is a short circuit": "When live and neutral wires touch directly, the resistance becomes very low and a very large current flows.",
  "what is overloading": "Too many appliances connected to a single socket draw excess current and may cause fire.",
  "what are the colour codes of household wires": "Live wire is red, neutral wire is black and earth wire is green (older: live red, neutral black).",
  "what is the supply voltage in india": "220 V at 50 Hz.",
  "what is the purpose of the earth wire": "It carries leakage current to the ground and protects users from shocks.",
  "what is an electric cell": "A device that converts chemical energy into electrical energy to maintain a potential difference.",
  "what is a battery": "A combination of two or more cells.",
  "what is the symbol of a resistor": "A zig-zag line or a small rectangle in a circuit diagram.",
  "what is the electric current in terms of electrons": "I = Q/t, where Q = ne with n the number of electrons and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C."
},

"13. Magnetic Effects of Electric Current": {
  "what is a magnetic field": "The region around a magnet in which its force can be detected.",
  "what are magnetic field lines": "Imaginary lines showing the direction of a magnetic field; they go from north to south outside the magnet.",
  "what are the properties of magnetic field lines": "They form closed curves, never intersect, run from N to S outside the magnet and are closer where the field is stronger.",
  "what is oersted's experiment": "In 1820 Oersted showed that a current in a wire deflects a compass needle, proving electricity produces magnetism.",
  "what is the right hand thumb rule": "Hold the wire in the right hand with the thumb along the current; the curled fingers show the direction of the magnetic field.",
  "what is the magnetic field due to a straight wire": "Concentric circles around the wire; the field increases with current and decreases with distance.",
  "what is the magnetic field due to a circular loop": "Concentric circles whose size increases away from the wire; at the centre the lines are straight.",
  "what is a solenoid in class 10": "A long coil of many circular turns of insulated wire; its field is like that of a bar magnet.",
  "what is an electromagnet": "A soft iron core in a solenoid acts as a strong temporary magnet when current flows.",
  "what factors affect an electromagnet": "Number of turns, current and the core material.",
  "what is the force on a current carrying conductor in a magnetic field": "A force acts on it that is maximum when the current is perpendicular to the field.",
  "what is fleming's left hand rule": "Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger at right angles: forefinger is the field, middle finger is the current and thumb is the force (motion).",
  "what is an electric motor": "A device that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy using the force on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field.",
  "what is the principle of an electric motor": "A current carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences a torque.",
  "what is a split ring commutator": "A device in a motor that reverses the direction of current in the coil every half rotation.",
  "what are brushes in a motor": "Carbon contacts that connect the commutator to the battery.",
  "what is the use of an electric motor": "Fans, washing machines, mixers, refrigerators and electric vehicles.",
  "what is electromagnetic induction in class 10": "Production of an induced current in a coil when the magnetic field around it changes.",
  "what is faraday's discovery": "A moving magnet near a coil induces a current in the coil.",
  "what is fleming's right hand rule": "The forefinger shows the field, thumb shows the motion of the conductor and the middle finger shows the induced current.",
  "what is an electric generator": "A device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by electromagnetic induction.",
  "what is the difference between ac and dc": "AC reverses direction periodically (50 Hz in India); DC flows in one direction.",
  "what are slip rings in a generator": "Rings that connect the rotating coil to the external circuit and give AC output.",
  "what is the advantage of ac": "AC can be transmitted over long distances with less energy loss.",
  "what are the safety devices in a domestic circuit": "Fuse, earth wire and miniature circuit breaker (MCB).",
  "how do you find the direction of the magnetic field with a compass": "The north end of the compass needle points in the direction of the field at that place.",
  "does the strength of the magnetic field depend on distance": "Yes, the field becomes weaker as one moves away from the conductor or magnet.",
  "what is a bar magnet field pattern": "Lines emerge from the north pole, curve around and enter the south pole, and run from S to N inside the magnet."
},

"14. Sources of Energy": {
  "what is a good source of energy": "One that gives a large amount of energy per unit mass or volume, is easy to store and transport, is safe, cheap and causes little pollution.",
  "what is a good fuel": "A fuel with high calorific value, a suitable ignition temperature, low smoke and easy availability.",
  "what is calorific value": "The amount of heat produced by complete burning of 1 kg of a fuel.",
  "what are conventional sources of energy": "Sources used for a long time: fossil fuels, hydro power and firewood.",
  "what are fossil fuels": "Coal, petroleum and natural gas formed from the buried remains of plants and animals over millions of years.",
  "what are the disadvantages of fossil fuels": "They are non-renewable and cause air pollution and global warming.",
  "what is a thermal power plant": "A plant that burns fossil fuels to heat water to steam, which drives turbines to produce electricity.",
  "what is a hydro power plant": "A plant that uses the kinetic energy of falling water from dams to rotate turbines and produce electricity.",
  "what are the disadvantages of dams": "They submerge land and villages, destroy ecosystems and displace people.",
  "what is biomass": "Plant and animal waste used as fuel, such as cow dung and wood.",
  "what is biogas": "A gas, mainly methane (up to 75%), produced by anaerobic decomposition of cow dung and plant waste, used as a clean fuel.",
  "what is a biogas plant": "A plant where slurry of cow dung is fermented by anaerobic bacteria; the leftover slurry is a good manure.",
  "what is wind energy": "Kinetic energy of wind used to turn the turbines of windmills that generate electricity.",
  "what are the limitations of wind energy": "Wind speed should be above 15 km/h, the sites are limited and the setup is costly.",
  "what is solar energy": "Energy from the Sun. The solar constant is about 1.4 kW/m².",
  "what is a solar cell": "A device that converts solar energy directly into electricity; made of silicon.",
  "what are the advantages of solar cells": "No moving parts, little maintenance, work in remote areas and cause no pollution.",
  "what are the limitations of solar cells": "Their cost is high and silicon of special grade is expensive.",
  "what is a solar cooker": "A device with a reflector and a black-painted box with glass cover that cooks food using sunlight.",
  "why are solar cookers painted black": "A black surface absorbs more heat.",
  "what is tidal energy": "Energy from the rise and fall of sea water, harnessed by building dams across the narrow sea openings.",
  "what is wave energy": "Energy from the kinetic energy of fast sea waves, used to turn turbines.",
  "what is ocean thermal energy": "Energy from the temperature difference between the surface and deep sea water.",
  "what is geothermal energy": "Heat from hot rocks inside the Earth that produces steam to run turbines.",
  "what is nuclear energy": "Energy released during nuclear fission or fusion according to E = mc².",
  "what are the problems of nuclear power": "Safe disposal of radioactive waste, high cost of plants and risk of accidents.",
  "what is nuclear fission in class 10": "The splitting of a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 into lighter nuclei with release of a huge amount of energy.",
  "what is nuclear fusion in class 10": "The joining of light nuclei like hydrogen to form a heavier nucleus with a huge release of energy, as in the Sun.",
  "what is the source of the sun's energy": "Nuclear fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium.",
  "what are renewable sources of energy": "Sources that can be replenished: solar, wind, hydro, tidal, biomass and geothermal energy.",
  "what are non-renewable sources of energy": "Sources that cannot be replaced quickly: coal, petroleum, natural gas and nuclear fuel."
},

"15. Our Environment": {
  "what is an ecosystem": "A community of living organisms interacting with each other and with the non-living environment.",
  "what are biotic and abiotic components": "Biotic components are living things (plants, animals, microbes); abiotic components are non-living things (water, air, soil, light, temperature).",
  "what are producers": "Green plants and algae that make food by photosynthesis; they trap solar energy.",
  "what are consumers": "Organisms that depend on others for food: herbivores, carnivores, omnivores and parasites.",
  "what are decomposers": "Bacteria and fungi that break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil.",
  "what is a food chain": "A sequence of organisms in which each one eats the one before it. Example: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle.",
  "what is a food web": "A network of many interconnected food chains in an ecosystem.",
  "what is a trophic level": "Each step in a food chain; producers are the first trophic level.",
  "what is the 10 percent law": "Only about 10 percent of the energy is passed to the next trophic level; the rest is lost as heat or used for life processes.",
  "why are food chains short": "Because energy decreases at each step, only 3 to 4 trophic levels can be supported.",
  "why does energy flow in one direction": "Energy captured by producers passes to higher levels and is not returned to the Sun or producers.",
  "what is biomagnification": "The increase in concentration of harmful non-biodegradable chemicals such as pesticides at higher trophic levels of a food chain.",
  "why is the concentration of pesticides highest in humans": "Humans are at the top of the food chain, so harmful chemicals accumulate in the body.",
  "what are biodegradable substances": "Wastes broken down by microorganisms, such as vegetable waste, paper and cotton.",

// PHYSICS & UNIT-CONVERSION GENERATOR
// Every answer below is computed by code from exact conversion
// factors and formulas, then stored as an ordinary question.
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
const convKeys = new Set();   // generated unit-conversion questions
const physKeys = new Set();   // generated physics numericals / facts
let pgCount = 0;

function pgPut(key, ans, kind) {
  if (key in qaBank) return false;
  qaBank[key] = ans;
  (kind === "c" ? convKeys : physKeys).add(key);
  pgCount++;
  return true;
}

// ---------- number formatting ----------
const PG_SUP = { "0":"⁰","1":"¹","2":"²","3":"³","4":"⁴","5":"⁵","6":"⁶","7":"⁷","8":"⁸","9":"⁹","-":"⁻" };
function pgFmt(x) {
  if (x === 0) return { s: "0", approx: false };
  const ax = Math.abs(x);
  const r = Number(x.toPrecision(7));
  const approx = Math.abs(x - r) > ax * 1e-9;
  let s;
  if (ax >= 1e9 || ax < 1e-5) {
    const [m, e] = x.toExponential(6).split("e");
    s = Number(m) + " × 10" + String(parseInt(e, 10)).split("").map(c => PG_SUP[c]).join("");
  } else {
    const str = String(Math.abs(r)), dot = str.indexOf(".");
    const ip = (dot < 0 ? str : str.slice(0, dot)).replace(/\B(?=(\d{3})+$)/g, ",");
    s = (r < 0 ? "-" : "") + ip + (dot < 0 ? "" : str.slice(dot));
  }
  return { s, approx };
}
const pgN  = x => pgFmt(x).s;
const pgAp = x => pgFmt(x).approx ? "approximately " : "";
// "5 metres", "1 metre", "approximately 0.3048 metres"
const pgQty = (x, sing, plur) => pgAp(x) + pgN(x) + " " + (Number(x.toPrecision(7)) === 1 ? sing : plur);
const pgNum = x => pgAp(x) + pgN(x);

// ---------- units ----------
// u(name, plural, factorToBase, [aliases])  aliases starting with ^ are case-sensitive
const PFX = [
  ["pico","p",-12],["nano","n",-9],["micro","µ",-6],["milli","m",-3],["centi","c",-2],["deci","d",-1],
  ["","",0],["kilo","k",3],["mega","M",6],["giga","G",9],["tera","T",12]
];
function pgU(n, p, f, al, note) { return { n, p: p || n + "s", f, al: al || [], note }; }
// prefixed family: base name/symbol, list of prefix names to use, extra aliases per prefix handled automatically
function pgFam(base, sym, prefixes, baseFactor) {
  baseFactor = baseFactor || 1;
  return prefixes.map(pn => {
    const px = PFX.find(x => x[0] === pn);
    const name = px[0] + base;
    const abbr = px[1] + sym;
    const al = [];
    // abbreviations: case-sensitive when milli/mega would clash, otherwise lowercase
    const clash = (px[1] === "M") || (px[1] === "m" && prefixes.includes("mega"));
    al.push(clash ? "^" + abbr : abbr.toLowerCase());
    if (px[1] === "µ") al.push("u" + sym.toLowerCase());
    return pgU(name, name + "s", baseFactor * Math.pow(10, px[2]), al);
  });
}

const PG_ALIAS = new Map();    // lowercase alias -> [{c, i}]

function pgAddAlias(map, a, ref) { if (!map.has(a)) map.set(a, []); map.get(a).push(ref); }

    names.forEach(a => {
      if (a.startsWith("^")) { pgAddAlias(PG_CS, a.slice(1), ref); return; }

  if (cat === "Temperature") return PG_TEMP[ib].from(PG_TEMP[ia].to(v));
  const L = PG_CATS[cat];
  return v * L[ia].f / L[ib].f;
}
function pgUnitName(cat, i, v) {
  const u = PG_CATS[cat][i];
  return Number(v.toPrecision(7)) === 1 ? u.n : u.p;
}
function pgConvAnswer(cat, ia, ib, v) {
  const r = pgConvertValue(cat, ia, ib, v);
  const ua = PG_CATS[cat][ia], ub = PG_CATS[cat][ib];
  let note = "";
  const notes = [ua.note, ub.note].filter(Boolean);
  if (notes.length) note = " (" + notes[0] + ")";
  if (cat === "Data" && (ua.n.endsWith("byte") && ua.n !== "byte" || ub.n.endsWith("byte") && ub.n !== "byte")) note = " (taking 1 kilobyte as 1024 bytes)";
  return `${pgN(v)} ${pgUnitName(cat, ia, v)} is equal to ${pgNum(r)} ${pgUnitName(cat, ib, r)}.${note}`;
}

// ---------- natural-language converter (any number, any phrasing) ----------
function pgResolve(str, wantCats) {
  let s = str.trim().replace(/μ/g, "µ").replace(/[.;:]+$/, "").replace(/^(?:the|an?|one|of)\s+/i, "");
  if (!s) return [];
  const cs = PG_CS.get(s);
  const l = s.toLowerCase();
  let res = cs ? cs.slice() : [];
  const tryKey = k => { const a = PG_ALIAS.get(k); if (a) a.forEach(r => res.push(r)); };
  tryKey(l);
  if (!res.length && l.endsWith("s")) tryKey(l.slice(0, -1));
  if (!res.length && l.endsWith("es")) tryKey(l.slice(0, -2));
  if (!res.length) { const t = l.replace(/^degrees?\s+/, ""); if (t !== l) tryKey(t); }
  return res;
}
function tryConvert(raw) {
  let q = raw.replace(/[?!]/g, " ").replace(/(\d),(?=\d{3}\b)/g, "$1").replace(/\s+/g, " ").trim();
  const NUM = "(-?\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?)";
  let guard = 0;
  while (guard++ < 4 && /^(please |jarvis |can you |could you |tell me |what is |what's |whats |how much is |calculate |find |give me |convert |change |express |hey )/i.test(q)) {
    q = q.replace(/^(please |jarvis |can you |could you |tell me |what is |what's |whats |how much is |calculate |find |give me |convert |change |express |hey )/i, "");
  }
  let m, v = 1, ua, ub;
  const art = "(?:an?|one|1)";
  if ((m = q.match(new RegExp("^how many (.+?) (?:are |is |do |does |will )?(?:there )?(?:in|make|equal to|are in) (?:" + art + "\\s+|" + NUM + "\\s*)?(.+)$", "i")))) {
    ub = m[1]; ua = m[3]; v = m[2] !== undefined ? parseFloat(m[2]) : 1;
  } else if ((m = q.match(new RegExp("^" + NUM + "\\s*(.+?) (?:is|are|=|equals?) how many (.+)$", "i")))) {
    v = parseFloat(m[1]); ua = m[2]; ub = m[3];
  } else if ((m = q.match(new RegExp("^" + NUM + "\\s*([a-z0-9µμåωΩ°²³/^.\\- ]+?)\\s+(?:to|in|into|equals?|equal to|=|as)\\s+(.+)$", "i")))) {
    v = parseFloat(m[1]); ua = m[2]; ub = m[3];
  } else if ((m = q.match(/^([a-z0-9µμåωΩ°²³/^.\- ]+?)\s+(?:to|in|into)\s+([a-z0-9µμåωΩ°²³/^.\- ]+)$/i))) {
    ua = m[1]; ub = m[2];
  } else return null;
  ub = ub.replace(/\s+(?:please|now)$/i, "");
  const A = pgResolve(ua), B = pgResolve(ub);
  if (!A.length || !B.length) return null;
  // find a pair in the same category
  let pair = null;
  for (const a of A) { for (const b of B) { if (a.c === b.c) { pair = [a, b]; break; } } if (pair) break; }
  if (!pair) {
    return `I can't convert ${ua.trim()} to ${ub.trim()}, Sir. They measure different things.`;
  }
  if (!isFinite(v)) return null;
  return pgConvAnswer(pair[0].c, pair[0].i, pair[1].i, v);
}

// ---------- generate conversion questions ----------
const PG_VALUES = [1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 1000];
const pgConvSample = [];
(function genConversions() {
  Object.keys(PG_CATS).forEach(cat => {
    const L = PG_CATS[cat];
    for (let a = 0; a < L.length; a++) {
      for (let b = 0; b < L.length; b++) {
        if (a === b) continue;
        if (cat !== "Temperature") {
          const ratio = L[a].f / L[b].f;
          if (ratio > 1e9 || ratio < 1e-9) continue;
        }
        const vals = cat === "Temperature" ? [-40, -10, 0, 10, 20, 25, 30, 37, 40, 50, 75, 98, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 400, 500, 1000] : PG_VALUES;
        vals.forEach(v => {
          const key = `convert ${v} ${v === 1 ? L[a].n : L[a].p} to ${L[b].p}`;
          if (pgPut(key, pgConvAnswer(cat, a, b, v), "c") && v === 1) pgConvSample.push(key);
        });
        // "how many X are in 1 Y" phrasing
        if (cat !== "Temperature") {
          const key2 = `how many ${L[b].p} are in 1 ${L[a].n}`;
          pgPut(key2, pgConvAnswer(cat, a, b, 1), "c");
        }
      }
    }
  });
})();

// ---------- physics numericals (formula-based, computed) ----------
const PG_G = 9.8;
function pgCart(lists, cb, i = 0, acc = []) {
  if (i === lists.length) { cb(...acc); return; }
  lists[i].forEach(x => pgCart(lists, cb, i + 1, acc.concat([x])));
}
const pgPhysSample = [];
const PG_SING = { kilograms:"kilogram", centimetres:"centimetre", amperes:"ampere", metres:"metre", seconds:"second", ohms:"ohm", newtons:"newton",
  litres:"litre", atmospheres:"atmosphere", hours:"hour", grams:"gram", volts:"volt", watts:"watt", joules:"joule", kilowatts:"kilowatt" };
function pgP(key, ans) {
  key = key.replace(/(^|[^\d.])1 (\w+)/g, (m, pre, w) => pre + "1 " + (PG_SING[w] || w));
  if (pgPut(key, ans, "p")) pgPhysSample.push(key);
}

(function genNumericals() {

    `Power = work ÷ time = ${w} ÷ ${t} = ${q(w/t,"watt","watts")}.`));

  pgCart([[1,2,3,4,5],[10,20,30,40,50],[2,4,5,10]], (p1, v1, p2) => pgP(`a gas at ${p1} atmospheres occupies ${v1} litres, what is its volume at ${p2} atmospheres at constant temperature`,
    `Boyle's law: P1 V1 = P2 V2, so V2 = ${p1} × ${v1} ÷ ${p2} = ${q(p1*v1/p2,"litre","litres")}.`));
  pgCart([[1,2,5,10,20],[250,273,300,350],[300,350,400,500,600]], (v1, t1, t2) => pgP(`a gas occupies ${v1} litres at ${t1} kelvin, what is its volume at ${t2} kelvin at constant pressure`,
    `Charles's law: V1 ÷ T1 = V2 ÷ T2, so V2 = ${v1} × ${t2} ÷ ${t1} = ${q(v1*t2/t1,"litre","litres")}.`));

  // Circular motion, pendulum, springs
  pgCart([[1,2,5,10,50],[2,4,5,10,20],[1,2,5,10,20]], (m, v, r) => pgP(`what is the centripetal force on a ${m} kilogram mass moving at ${v} metres per second in a circle of radius ${r} metres`,
    `F = m v² ÷ r = ${m} × ${v}² ÷ ${r} = ${q(m*v*v/r,"newton","newtons")}.`));
  [1,2,3,4,5,10,25,100].forEach(l => {
    pgP(`what is the time period of a simple pendulum of length ${l} metres`, `T = 2π √(l ÷ g) = 2π √(${l} ÷ 9.8) = ${q(2*Math.PI*Math.sqrt(l/PG_G),"second","seconds")}.`);
    pgP(`what is the frequency of a simple pendulum of length ${l} metres`, `f = 1 ÷ T = 1 ÷ (2π √(${l} ÷ 9.8)) = ${q(1/(2*Math.PI*Math.sqrt(l/PG_G)),"hertz","hertz")}.`);
  });
  pgCart([[10,20,50,100,200,500,1000,2000],[1,2,5,10,20,30,50]], (k, x) => {
    pgP(`what is the force in a spring of stiffness ${k} newtons per metre stretched by ${x} centimetres`, `F = k x = ${k} × ${x/100} = ${q(k*x/100,"newton","newtons")}.`);
    pgP(`what is the energy stored in a spring of stiffness ${k} newtons per metre stretched by ${x} centimetres`, `E = ½ k x² = ½ × ${k} × ${x/100}² = ${q(0.5*k*(x/100)**2,"joule","joules")}.`);
  });

  // Machines and efficiency
  [50,100,200,500,1000].forEach(inp => [10,20,25,40,50,60,75,80,90,150,200,400].forEach(out => { if (out < inp)
    pgP(`what is the efficiency of a machine with ${inp} joules of input energy and ${out} joules of useful output`, `Efficiency = (output ÷ input) × 100 = (${out} ÷ ${inp}) × 100 = ${pgNum(out/inp*100)} percent.`); }));
  [10,20,50,100,200].forEach(L => [1,2,5,10].forEach(la => [2,5,10,20,50].forEach(ea => { if (ea > la)
    pgP(`a load of ${L} newtons is ${la} metres from the fulcrum, what effort is needed at ${ea} metres to balance it`, `Effort × effort arm = load × load arm, so effort = ${L} × ${la} ÷ ${ea} = ${q(L*la/ea,"newton","newtons")}.`); })));
  [3,4,5,6,8,9,12,15].forEach(a => [3,4,5,6,8,9,12,15].forEach(b => { if (a <= b)
    pgP(`what is the resultant of two perpendicular forces of ${a} newtons and ${b} newtons`, `R = √(${a}² + ${b}²) = √${a*a+b*b} = ${q(Math.sqrt(a*a+b*b),"newton","newtons")}.`); }));

  // Modern physics
  [1,2,5,10,50,100,500,1000].forEach(g =>
    pgP(`how much energy is released when ${g} grams of mass is completely converted into energy`, `E = m c² = ${g/1000} × (3 × 10⁸)² = ${q(g/1000*9e16,"joule","joules")}.`));
})();

    });
  });
})();

// ---------- topic chips for the generated questions ----------
(function pgGroups() {
  const every = (arr, n) => { const step = Math.max(1, Math.floor(arr.length / n)); return arr.filter((_, i) => i % step === 0).slice(0, n); };
  const si = [], consts = [];
  physKeys.forEach(k => {
    if (k.startsWith("what is the si unit of ")) si.push(k);
    else if (k.startsWith("what is the value of ") && !k.startsWith("what is the value of the prefix")) consts.push(k);
  });
  chapterKeys["Unit Conversions"] = every(pgConvSample, 90);
  chapterKeys["Physics Numericals"] = every(pgPhysSample, 90);
  chapterKeys["SI Units"] = si;
  chapterKeys["Physical Constants"] = consts;
})();

// CLASS 10 SCIENCE MEGA-PACK
// Answers are computed by code from formulas and fixed tables.
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
const c10Gen = new Set();   // keys whose numbers must match exactly
(function c10Pack() {
  const G = {};
  const f = x => { const r = +x.toFixed(2); return (Math.abs(x - r) > 1e-9 ? "approximately " : "") + r; };
  const put = (g, k, a, gen) => { if (k in qaBank) return; qaBank[k] = a; class10Keys.add(k); if (gen) c10Gen.add(k); (G[g] = G[g] || []).push(k); };
  const tbl = s => s.split(";").map(r => r.split("|"));

  // ── Electricity numericals ──
  const E = "Numericals: Electricity";
  const Is = [0.1,0.2,0.25,0.5,0.75,1,1.5,2,2.5,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,15,20,25,30];
  const Rs = [1,2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,15,20,25,30,40,50,60,75,100,120,150,200,220,250,300,500];
  const Vs = [1.5,3,4.5,5,6,9,10,12,24,36,100,110,220,230,240];
  Is.forEach(i => Rs.forEach(r => put(E, `a current of ${i} A flows through a resistor of ${r} ohm what is the potential difference across it`, `V = I × R = ${i} × ${r} = ${f(i*r)} V.`, 1)));
  Vs.forEach(v => Rs.forEach(r => put(E, `a potential difference of ${v} V is applied across a resistor of ${r} ohm what is the current`, `I = V / R = ${v} / ${r} = ${f(v/r)} A.`, 1)));
  Vs.forEach(v => Is.forEach(i => put(E, `a current of ${i} A flows when the potential difference is ${v} V what is the resistance`, `R = V / I = ${v} / ${i} = ${f(v/i)} ohm.`, 1)));
  Vs.forEach(v => Is.slice(0, 15).forEach(i => put(E, `an appliance works on ${v} V and draws ${i} A what is its power`, `P = V × I = ${v} × ${i} = ${f(v*i)} W.`, 1)));
  const Ps = [5,10,15,20,40,60,75,100,500,1000,1500,2000];
  [12,110,220,230,240].forEach(v => Ps.forEach(p => put(E, `an appliance of power ${p} W works on ${v} V what current does it draw`, `I = P / V = ${p} / ${v} = ${f(p/v)} A.`, 1)));
  Ps.forEach(p => [1,2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,24].forEach(h => put(E, `how much electrical energy in kWh is used by a ${p} W appliance running for ${h} hours`, `E = P × t = ${p} W × ${h} h = ${f(p*h/1000)} kWh (units).`, 1)));
  [0.5,1,2,3,4,5].forEach(i => [2,5,10,20,50,100].forEach(r => [1,2,5,10,30,60].forEach(t => put(E, `how much heat is produced when a current of ${i} A flows through a resistor of ${r} ohm for ${t} s`, `H = I²Rt = ${i}² × ${r} × ${t} = ${f(i*i*r*t)} J.`, 1))));
  const Rl = [1,2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,15,20,25,30,40,50,60,75,100,150,200];
  Rl.forEach((a, x) => Rl.slice(x).forEach(b => {
