what is artificial intelligence|Artificial intelligence is the ability of machines to perform tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognising images and making decisions.
what is machine learning|Machine learning is a branch of AI in which computers learn patterns from data instead of being programmed with fixed rules.
what is deep learning|Deep learning is machine learning that uses many-layered neural networks to learn complex patterns from large amounts of data.
what is a neural network|A neural network is a computing model made of connected layers of nodes, loosely inspired by the brain, that learns from data.
what is a large language model|A large language model is an AI trained on huge amounts of text to understand and generate language.
what is generative ai|Generative AI creates new content such as text, images, audio or code from patterns it learned in training data.
what is a chatbot|A chatbot is a program that converses with people through text or voice.
what is a prompt|A prompt is the instruction or question you give to an AI system.
what is prompt engineering|Prompt engineering is the practice of writing clear, specific instructions to get better results from an AI.
what is cloud computing|Cloud computing means using servers on the internet to store data and run programs instead of using only your own device.
what is the internet of things|The Internet of Things is a network of everyday devices, like smart bulbs and watches, that connect to the internet and share data.
what is cyber security|Cyber security is protecting computers, networks and data from attacks.
what is a vpn|A VPN (virtual private network) encrypts your internet connection and hides your IP address.
what is an ip address|An IP address is a unique number that identifies a device on a network.
what is a domain name|A domain name is the human-readable address of a website, such as example.com.
what is ssl|SSL, now TLS, is a protocol that encrypts data between your browser and a website; you see it as https.
what is the difference between http and https|HTTPS is HTTP with encryption, so data sent between you and the site is protected.
what is open source|Open source software has its source code publicly available for anyone to view, use and modify.
what is an api|An API (application programming interface) lets one program talk to another.
what is a database|A database is an organised collection of data that can be stored, searched and updated.
what is sql|SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language used to work with relational databases.
what is a variable in programming|A variable is a named place in memory that stores a value.
what is a function in programming|A function is a reusable block of code that performs a specific task.
what is a loop in programming|A loop repeats a block of code until a condition is met.
what is an array|An array is an ordered collection of items stored under one name.
what is object oriented programming|Object-oriented programming organises code into objects that combine data and the functions that work on it.
what is recursion|Recursion is when a function calls itself to solve smaller parts of a problem.
what is debugging|Debugging is finding and fixing errors in a program.
what is git|Git is a version control system that tracks changes to code and helps people collaborate.
what is github|GitHub is a website for hosting Git repositories and collaborating on code.
what is the best programming language to learn first|Python is a popular first choice because its syntax is simple and readable; JavaScript is great if you want to build websites.
how to learn coding|Pick one language such as Python, learn the basics, build small projects, read other people's code and practise daily.
what is a smartphone|A smartphone is a mobile phone with computer-like features such as internet access, apps and a camera.
what is 5g|5G is the fifth generation of mobile networks, offering faster speeds and lower delay than 4G.
what is bluetooth|Bluetooth is a short-range wireless technology for connecting devices such as earphones and speakers.
what is nfc|NFC (near field communication) lets devices exchange data when they are very close, used for contactless payments.
what is upi|UPI (Unified Payments Interface) is an instant payment system in India that lets you send money using a mobile app.
what is gst|GST (Goods and Services Tax) is an indirect tax charged on the supply of goods and services in India.
what is a pan card|A PAN card carries a Permanent Account Number issued by the Income Tax Department for tax purposes in India.
what is an aadhaar card|Aadhaar is a 12-digit identity number issued to residents of India by the UIDAI.

how many calories should i eat a day|Most adults need roughly 1,800 to 2,500 calories a day depending on age, sex, weight and activity. A doctor or dietitian can give a personal figure.
how much protein do i need a day|A common guideline is about 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight for adults, more for athletes. A dietitian can personalise this.
how much water should i drink a day|Most adults do well with about 2 to 3 litres of fluids a day, more in hot weather or when exercising.
how many hours of sleep do i need|Adults generally need 7 to 9 hours of sleep and teenagers 8 to 10 hours.
how to lose belly fat|There is no way to target belly fat alone; a balanced diet, regular exercise, enough sleep and a steady calorie deficit reduce overall fat.
how to build muscle|Lift weights progressively, eat enough protein and calories, sleep well and stay consistent for months.
how to improve immunity|Eat a balanced diet, sleep well, exercise, manage stress, stay vaccinated and avoid smoking.
how to reduce stress|Try deep breathing, exercise, enough sleep, short breaks, talking to someone you trust and limiting caffeine.
how to stop overthinking|Write your thoughts down, focus on what you can control, take a walk, limit social media and talk to someone you trust.
how to wake up early|Sleep at a fixed time, avoid screens before bed, keep your alarm across the room and get sunlight soon after waking.
how to improve concentration|Remove distractions, work in short focused blocks with breaks, sleep well and exercise.
how to study effectively|Set goals, use active recall and spaced revision, practise past questions, take breaks and sleep well.
how to learn english fast|Speak and listen daily, read short texts, learn words in context, write a little each day and don't fear mistakes.
how to improve communication skills|Listen actively, speak clearly and slowly, ask questions, read widely and practise in real conversations.
how to be confident|Prepare well, practise speaking up, set small challenges, look after your body and learn from mistakes.
how to make money online|Common options are freelancing, tutoring, content creation, selling products and remote jobs. Avoid anything that asks you to pay upfront for guaranteed income.
how to save money|Track your spending, set a budget, save first and spend after, avoid impulse purchases and build an emergency fund.
how to invest money|Build an emergency fund first, then consider diversified options such as index mutual funds through SIPs. I am not a financial advisor, so check with one for personal advice.
what is the difference between saving and investing|Saving keeps money safe and accessible, usually in a bank, while investing puts money in assets like shares or funds to grow over time, with more risk.
what is a mutual fund|A mutual fund pools money from many investors and invests it in shares, bonds or other assets managed by professionals.
what is the stock market|The stock market is where shares of companies are bought and sold.
what is a sip|A SIP is a way to invest a fixed amount in a mutual fund at regular intervals.
what is compound interest|Compound interest is interest earned on both the original amount and the interest already added.
what is credit score|A credit score, such as CIBIL in India, is a number that shows how reliably you repay loans; 750 and above is generally considered good.
what is a budget|A budget is a plan for how you will earn, spend and save money.
what is cryptocurrency|Cryptocurrency is digital money secured by cryptography and not controlled by a central bank; its value can be very volatile.
what is bitcoin|Bitcoin is the first and best-known cryptocurrency, created in 2009 by a person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto.
how to tie a tie|Cross the wide end over the narrow end, wrap it behind and around, bring it up through the neck loop, down through the front knot, then tighten and adjust.
how to boil an egg|Place eggs in boiling water; cook about 6 minutes for soft, 9 for medium and 12 for hard-boiled, then cool in cold water.
how to make tea|Boil water, add tea leaves, simmer a couple of minutes, add milk and sugar if you like, then strain and serve.
how to make coffee|Add ground coffee to a cup or filter, pour hot water just off the boil and let it brew for a few minutes.
how to make maggi|Boil about 1.5 cups of water, add the noodles and tastemaker, cook 2 to 3 minutes and serve hot.
how to cook rice|Rinse the rice, add about two parts water to one part rice, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer on low for 15 to 20 minutes.
how to make omelette|Beat eggs with salt and pepper, pour into a hot oiled pan, add chopped onion and chilli if you like, and cook until set, folding once.
how to make pasta|Boil salted water, cook the pasta for the time on the packet, drain and mix with your sauce.
how to make pizza at home|Make or buy dough, roll it out, spread sauce, add cheese and toppings, and bake at about 220 degrees Celsius for 10 to 15 minutes.
how to make a paper plane|Fold a sheet in half lengthwise, fold the top corners to the centre, fold the new edges to the centre again, fold in half and fold down the wings.
how to tie shoelaces|Cross the laces, tuck one under and pull tight, make a loop with each lace, cross the loops and pull them through, then tighten.
how to wash hands properly|Wet your hands, apply soap, rub palms, backs, between fingers and under nails for at least 20 seconds, rinse and dry.
how to brush teeth properly|Brush twice a day for two minutes with a soft brush and fluoride toothpaste, covering all surfaces, and floss daily.
how to take a screenshot on windows|Press the Windows key with Shift and S, or press Print Screen.
how to take a screenshot on iphone|Press the side button and the volume up button together on newer iPhones.
how to take a screenshot on android|Press the power and volume down buttons together.
how to copy and paste|Select the text, press Ctrl+C (Cmd+C on Mac) to copy, then Ctrl+V (Cmd+V) to paste.
how to undo on a computer|Press Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac).
how to restart a computer|Open the Start menu, choose Power, then Restart, or press and hold the power button if it is frozen.
how to speed up a slow computer|Close unused programs, restart, free up disk space, uninstall unused apps, scan for malware and consider adding RAM or an SSD.
how to charge a phone faster|Use the original charger and cable, turn on airplane mode, switch the screen off and avoid heavy use while charging.
how to increase phone battery life|Lower screen brightness, close background apps, turn off unused connections and keep the software updated.
how to make a resume|Put your contact details, a short summary, education, skills and experience in clear sections, keep it to one page and tailor it to the job.
how to write an email|Use a clear subject, greet politely, state your purpose briefly, and end with thanks and your name.
how to write an essay|Plan an outline, write an introduction with your main point, develop paragraphs with evidence, and finish with a conclusion.
how to prepare for an interview|Research the company, practise common questions, prepare examples of your work, dress neatly and arrive early.
how to crack upsc|Understand the syllabus, read NCERTs first, follow a daily routine, read newspapers, practise answer writing and take mock tests.
how to prepare for jee|Master NCERT concepts, practise many problems daily, take regular mock tests, revise weak topics and keep a steady schedule.
how to prepare for neet|Study NCERT biology thoroughly, practise chemistry and physics numericals, take mock tests and revise regularly.
how to start a youtube channel|Choose a topic, create a channel, make a few quality videos with good audio, upload consistently and learn from your analytics.
how to start a business|Find a real problem to solve, test your idea cheaply, make a simple plan, register the business and learn from customers.
how to learn guitar|Learn the basic chords, practise short sessions daily, use a tuner and play along with simple songs.
how to meditate|Sit comfortably, close your eyes, breathe slowly and bring your attention back to your breath whenever it wanders, starting with 5 minutes a day.
how to do yoga for beginners|Start with simple poses like mountain pose, cat-cow, child's pose and downward dog, breathing slowly, for 15 to 20 minutes a day.
how to swim|Learn in shallow water with an instructor, practise floating, kicking and breathing, then add arm strokes.
how to ride a bicycle|Start on flat ground with a helmet, practise balancing and gliding, then pedal while looking ahead.
how to drive a car|Take lessons from a licensed instructor, learn the controls, practise in empty areas first and always follow traffic rules.
how to renew a driving licence in india|Apply on the Parivahan Sarathi website or at your RTO with your old licence and required documents.
how to apply for a passport in india|Register on the Passport Seva portal, fill in the form, book an appointment and visit the Passport Seva Kendra with your documents.
how to link aadhaar with pan|Use the Income Tax e-filing portal's Link Aadhaar option, enter your PAN and Aadhaar numbers and pay the fee if required.
how to check pan card status|Use the NSDL or UTIITSL website's application status option with your acknowledgement number.
how to file income tax return|Log in to the Income Tax e-filing portal, choose the right ITR form, fill in your income and deductions, and e-verify.
what is the capital of india|New Delhi is the capital of India.

what is the national sport of india|India has no officially declared national sport; hockey is often called the national game.
what is the national song of india|Vande Mataram.
what is the national anthem of india|Jana Gana Mana.
what is the national calendar of india|The Saka calendar.
what is the national currency symbol of india|The rupee symbol ₹.
what is the longest river in india|The Ganga is the longest river that flows within India.
what is the highest mountain peak in india|Kangchenjunga is the highest peak entirely in India.
what is the largest state in india by area|Rajasthan.
what is the smallest state in india by area|Goa.
what is the most populated state in india|Uttar Pradesh.

what is the longest railway platform in india|Gorakhpur railway station has one of the longest platforms in the world.

what is the biggest desert in india|The Thar Desert.

what is the first satellite of india|Aryabhata, launched in 1975.
when did india get independence|India became independent on 15 August 1947.
when was the indian constitution adopted|The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950.
who was the first president of india|Dr Rajendra Prasad.
who was the first prime minister of india|Jawaharlal Nehru.
who was the first woman president of india|Pratibha Patil.
who was the first woman prime minister of india|Indira Gandhi.
how many lok sabha seats are there|The Lok Sabha has 543 elected seats.
how many rajya sabha seats are there|The Rajya Sabha has a maximum of 250 members, with 245 at present.
what is the minimum age to vote in india|18 years.
what is the minimum age to become president of india|35 years.
how many fundamental rights are there in india|The Indian Constitution gives six fundamental rights.
how many articles are in the indian constitution|The original Constitution had 395 articles; it now has about 470 after amendments, organised in 25 parts.
which is the largest country in the world|Russia is the largest country by area.
which is the smallest country in the world|Vatican City.
which is the most populated country in the world|India is the most populous country in the world.
which is the longest river in the world|The Nile and the Amazon are the two contenders, with the Nile traditionally listed as the longest.
which is the highest mountain in the world|Mount Everest, about 8,849 metres above sea level.
which is the largest ocean|The Pacific Ocean.
which is the largest desert in the world|Antarctica is the largest desert; the Sahara is the largest hot desert.
which is the deepest point in the ocean|The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, nearly 11,000 metres deep.
which is the largest continent|Asia.
which is the smallest continent|Australia (Oceania).
how many countries are there in the world|There are 195 countries: 193 United Nations members plus two observer states, the Holy See and Palestine.
how many continents are there|There are seven continents: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia.
how many oceans are there|There are five oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic.
how many time zones are there in the world|There are 24 standard time zones, though some places use half-hour offsets.
how many time zones does india have|India uses a single time zone, Indian Standard Time, which is UTC+5:30.
what is the tallest building in the world|The Burj Khalifa in Dubai, about 828 metres tall.
what is the longest wall in the world|The Great Wall of China.
what are the seven wonders of the world|The new seven wonders are the Great Wall of China, Petra, Christ the Redeemer, Machu Picchu, Chichen Itza, the Colosseum and the Taj Mahal.
what is the biggest animal in the world|The blue whale.
what is the fastest animal in the world|The peregrine falcon in a dive is the fastest animal; the cheetah is the fastest on land.
what is the tallest animal|The giraffe.
what is the largest land animal|The African elephant.
what is the smallest bird|The bee hummingbird.
what is the largest bird|The ostrich.
which animal is the king of the jungle|The lion.
which animal can sleep standing|The horse can sleep while standing.
which is the only mammal that can fly|The bat.
how many legs does a spider have|A spider has eight legs.
how many legs does an insect have|An insect has six legs.
how many hearts does an octopus have|An octopus has three hearts.
how long do elephants live|Elephants live about 60 to 70 years in the wild.
how long do dogs live|Most dogs live about 10 to 15 years, depending on breed and size.
how long do cats live|Indoor cats often live 12 to 18 years.
how many bones does a human have|An adult human has 206 bones.
how many teeth does an adult have|An adult normally has 32 teeth.
how many chambers does the human heart have|Four.
how many litres of blood are in the human body|An adult has about 5 litres of blood.
what is the largest organ of the human body|The skin.
what is the smallest bone in the human body|The stapes in the ear.
what is the strongest muscle in the human body|The masseter (jaw muscle) is often called the strongest for its size, and the gluteus maximus is the largest.
what is the normal body temperature|About 37 degrees Celsius or 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit.
what is the normal heart rate|About 60 to 100 beats per minute at rest for adults.
what is normal blood pressure|About 120/80 mm Hg.
what is a normal blood sugar level|A fasting blood sugar of about 70 to 99 mg/dL is generally considered normal.
what causes hiccups|Hiccups are caused by sudden involuntary contractions of the diaphragm, often after eating or drinking quickly.
why do we yawn|The exact reason is unclear; theories include cooling the brain, regulating alertness and keeping the lungs open.
why do we dream|Scientists think dreams relate to memory processing and emotion regulation during sleep, but the full reason is not known.
why do we sneeze|Sneezing is a reflex that clears irritants from the nose.
why do we get goosebumps|Tiny muscles at the base of hair follicles contract, a leftover reflex that once helped fluff up fur for warmth.
why is the ocean salty|Rivers carry dissolved minerals from rocks into the sea, and when water evaporates the salts stay behind.
why is the sky blue|Air molecules scatter short blue wavelengths of sunlight more than longer red wavelengths.
why is the sea blue|Water absorbs red light more than blue, and the sky's reflection adds to the blue colour.
why is grass green|Grass contains chlorophyll, which absorbs red and blue light and reflects green.
why do leaves change colour in autumn|Chlorophyll breaks down, revealing yellow and orange pigments that were hidden underneath.
why do we have seasons|Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.5 degrees as it orbits the Sun.
why does the moon change shape|We see different amounts of the Moon's sunlit half as it orbits the Earth.
why do stars twinkle|Atmospheric turbulence bends starlight and makes it flicker.
why does ice float on water|Ice is less dense than liquid water because water molecules form an open lattice when they freeze.
why does a rainbow form|Sunlight is refracted, reflected and dispersed by water droplets into its colours.
why is the sun hot|The Sun's core fuses hydrogen into helium, releasing enormous energy.
why is mars red|Iron oxide, or rust, on its surface gives it a red colour.
why can't we hear sound in space|Sound needs a medium to travel through, and space is nearly a vacuum.
why do we have a leap year|Earth takes about 365.25 days to orbit the Sun, so an extra day every four years keeps the calendar aligned.
why is the leaning tower of pisa leaning|Its foundation was built on soft soil that settled unevenly.
how do planes fly|Wings create lift because air moves faster over the curved top, reducing pressure, while engines provide thrust.
how do magnets work|Magnetic fields come from moving electric charges and aligned electron spins in materials like iron.
how does a battery work|A battery converts chemical energy to electrical energy through reactions at two electrodes.
how does wifi work|A router sends data as radio waves to your device, which sends data back the same way.
how does gps work|A device calculates its position from the timing of signals from several satellites.
how does a microwave work|It produces microwaves that make water molecules in food vibrate, which heats the food.
how does a refrigerator work|A refrigerant absorbs heat inside the fridge and releases it outside as it is compressed and expanded.
how does a vaccine work|A vaccine trains the immune system to recognise a germ so it can respond quickly if you are exposed.
how does the internet work|Devices exchange small packets of data over networks linked together using common protocols.
how does a solar panel work|Solar cells convert sunlight into electricity through the photovoltaic effect.
how does a rainbow form|Water droplets refract, reflect and disperse sunlight into its colours.
how does a rocket work|It expels hot gas downward at high speed, and by Newton's third law is pushed upward.
how does the heart work|The heart pumps blood through the body by contracting its four chambers in sequence.
how do birds fly|Birds generate lift with their curved wings and thrust by flapping them.
how are mountains formed|Most mountains form when tectonic plates collide and push the crust upward; others come from volcanoes or faulting.
how are earthquakes caused|They are caused by sudden release of energy along faults in Earth's crust.
how are volcanoes formed|They form where magma rises through the crust, often at plate boundaries or hot spots.
how is rain formed|Water evaporates, rises, cools and condenses into clouds, and the droplets grow heavy and fall.
how is thunder produced|Lightning heats the air so rapidly that it expands and creates a shock wave we hear as thunder.
how is glass made|Sand is melted with soda ash and limestone at very high temperature and then cooled.
how is paper made|Wood pulp is mixed with water, pressed into sheets and dried.
how is cheese made|Milk is curdled, the curds are separated from the whey, pressed and often aged.
how is chocolate made|Cocoa beans are fermented, dried, roasted, ground and mixed with sugar and cocoa butter.
how is sugar made|Juice from sugarcane or sugar beet is extracted, purified and crystallised.
how is salt made|Salt is obtained by evaporating seawater or mining rock salt.
how is steel made|Iron is refined with carbon and other elements in a furnace.
how is electricity generated|Mostly by turning turbines using steam, water or wind, which spin generators.
what is the speed of light|About 299,792 kilometres per second in a vacuum.
what is the speed of sound|About 343 metres per second in air at 20 degrees Celsius.
what is the boiling point of water|100 degrees Celsius at standard pressure.
what is the freezing point of water|0 degrees Celsius.
what is the melting point of ice|0 degrees Celsius.
what is the hottest planet|Venus is the hottest planet.
what is the coldest planet|Uranus has the coldest recorded atmosphere.
what is the closest star to earth|The Sun; the nearest star after that is Proxima Centauri.
what is the largest planet|Jupiter.
what is the smallest planet|Mercury.
what is a black hole|A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.
what is the big bang|The Big Bang theory says the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding since.
what is the milky way|The Milky Way is the galaxy that contains our solar system.
what is a light year|A light year is the distance light travels in a year, about 9.46 trillion kilometres.
what is the age of the earth|About 4.5 billion years.
what is the age of the universe|About 13.8 billion years.
how far is the moon from the earth|About 384,400 kilometres.
how far is the sun from the earth|About 150 million kilometres.
how long does light from the sun take to reach earth|About 8 minutes and 20 seconds.
how long does it take to go to mars|With current rockets, a trip takes roughly six to nine months.
did humans land on the moon|Yes. Apollo 11 landed the first humans on the Moon in 1969, and six crewed landings in total were made between 1969 and 1972.
who was the first person on the moon|Neil Armstrong in 1969.
who was the first person in space|Yuri Gagarin in 1961.
who was the first indian in space|Rakesh Sharma in 1984.
what is isro|ISRO is the Indian Space Research Organisation, India's space agency.
what is chandrayaan 3|Chandrayaan-3 was India's lunar mission that landed near the Moon's south pole in August 2023.
what is aditya l1|Aditya-L1 is India's first space mission to study the Sun, launched in 2023.
what is gaganyaan|Gaganyaan is India's human spaceflight programme.
what are the colours of the rainbow|Violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red.
what are the primary colours|The primary colours of light are red, green and blue; for pigments they are traditionally red, yellow and blue.
what are the secondary colours|Orange, green and purple are the secondary colours made by mixing primary pigment colours.
what colour do you get by mixing red and blue|Mixing red and blue gives purple.
what colour do you get by mixing yellow and blue|Mixing yellow and blue gives green.
what colour do you get by mixing red and yellow|Mixing red and yellow gives orange.
how many days are in a year|A normal year has 365 days; a leap year has 366.
how many weeks are in a year|There are 52 weeks in a year.
how many seconds are in a day|There are 86,400 seconds in a day.
how many minutes are in a day|There are 1,440 minutes in a day.
how many hours are in a week|There are 168 hours in a week.
how many days until new year|Check your calendar for the exact number; the new year begins on 1 January.
what is a leap year|A leap year has 366 days, with an extra day, 29 February, added roughly every four years.
what is the date today|I can tell you today's date from your device clock: just ask me what the date is.
what is a decade|A decade is a period of 10 years.
what is a century|A century is a period of 100 years.
what is a millennium|A millennium is a period of 1,000 years.
what is a dozen|A dozen is 12.
what is a gross|A gross is 144, or twelve dozen.
what is a score|A score is 20, as in four score and seven years.
what is a lakh|A lakh is 100,000.
what is a crore|A crore is 10,000,000, or 100 lakh.
what is an arab|An arab is 1,000,000,000, or 100 crore, in the Indian numbering system.
what is the value of pi|Pi is approximately 3.14159.
what is the value of e|Euler's number e is approximately 2.71828.
what is the golden ratio|The golden ratio is about 1.618.
what is zero|Zero is the number representing nothing; it is neither positive nor negative.
what is infinity|Infinity is an unbounded quantity larger than any number, written ∞.
what is a prime number|A prime number is greater than 1 and has exactly two factors, 1 and itself.
what is a perfect number|A perfect number equals the sum of its proper divisors; 6 and 28 are examples.
what is the fibonacci sequence|A sequence where each number is the sum of the two before it: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 and so on.
what is the pythagorean theorem|In a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides.
what is the quadratic formula|x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a for ax² + bx + c = 0.
what is the area of a circle|Area = πr².
what is the circumference of a circle|Circumference = 2πr.
what is the area of a triangle|Area = ½ × base × height.
what is the volume of a sphere|Volume = 4/3 πr³.
what is the formula for speed|Speed = distance ÷ time.
what is the formula for density|Density = mass ÷ volume.
what is the formula for force|Force = mass × acceleration.
what is the formula for work|Work = force × displacement.
what is the formula for power|Power = work ÷ time.
what is the formula for pressure|Pressure = force ÷ area.
what is the formula for kinetic energy|KE = ½mv².
what is the formula for potential energy|PE = mgh.
what is the formula for ohms law|V = IR.
what is the formula for water|The chemical formula of water is H₂O.
what is the formula for salt|The chemical formula of common salt is NaCl.
what is the formula for sugar|Table sugar (sucrose) is C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁.
what is the formula for carbon dioxide|CO₂.
what is the formula for ammonia|NH₃.
what is the formula for methane|CH₄.
what is the formula for baking soda|NaHCO₃.
what is the formula for vinegar|Vinegar is a solution of acetic acid, CH₃COOH.
what is the formula for ozone|O₃.
what is the formula for hydrogen peroxide|H₂O₂.
what is the full form of dna|Deoxyribonucleic acid.
what is the full form of rna|Ribonucleic acid.
what is the full form of atp|Adenosine triphosphate.
what is the difference between weather and climate|Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere; climate is the average weather over many years.
what is the difference between speed and velocity|Speed is how fast something moves; velocity is speed with a direction.
what is the difference between mass and weight|Mass is the amount of matter in an object; weight is the force of gravity on it.
what is the difference between a virus and bacteria|Bacteria are living single-celled organisms that can live on their own; viruses are much smaller and can reproduce only inside host cells.
what is the difference between an atom and a molecule|An atom is the smallest unit of an element; a molecule is two or more atoms bonded together.
what is the difference between a star and a planet|A star makes its own light through nuclear fusion; a planet orbits a star and shines by reflected light.
what is the difference between ai and machine learning|AI is the broad goal of making machines intelligent; machine learning is one method that lets computers learn from data.
what is the difference between hardware and software|Hardware is the physical parts of a computer; software is the programs that run on it.
what is the difference between ram and rom|RAM is temporary working memory; ROM is permanent memory that holds start-up instructions.
what is the difference between a crocodile and an alligator|Crocodiles have a pointed V-shaped snout and show their lower teeth; alligators have a rounded U-shaped snout.
what is the difference between a frog and a toad|Frogs have smooth, moist skin and live near water; toads have dry, bumpy skin and spend more time on land.
what is the difference between a fruit and a vegetable|Botanically, fruits develop from a flower's ovary and contain seeds, while vegetables are other plant parts such as roots, stems and leaves.
what is the difference between a disease and a disorder|A disease usually has a specific cause such as an infection, while a disorder is a disruption of normal function that may have varied causes.
what is the difference between an epidemic and a pandemic|An epidemic spreads in a region; a pandemic spreads across many countries or continents.
what is the difference between sympathy and empathy|Sympathy is feeling sorry for someone; empathy is sharing and understanding their feelings.
what is the difference between affect and effect|Affect is usually a verb meaning to influence; effect is usually a noun meaning a result.
what is the difference between its and it's|Its shows possession; it's means it is or it has.
what is the difference between their there and they're|Their shows possession, there refers to a place, and they're means they are.
what is the difference between a simile and a metaphor|A simile compares using like or as; a metaphor says one thing is another.
what is the difference between a noun and a pronoun|A noun names a person, place or thing; a pronoun replaces a noun.

const gkKeys = new Set();
(function gkPack() {
  const G = {};
  const put = (g, k, a) => { k = k.toLowerCase(); if (k in qaBank) return; qaBank[k] = a; gkKeys.add(k); (G[g] = G[g] || []).push(k); };
  const rows = s => s.trim().split("\n").map(r => r.trim()).filter(Boolean).map(r => r.split("|"));
  const lines = (g, s) => rows(s).forEach(r => put(g, r[0], r.slice(1).join("|")));
  const wrote = (g, s) => rows(s).forEach(([b, a]) => { put(g, "who wrote " + b, `${b} was written by ${a}.`); });
  const did = (g, s) => rows(s).forEach(([v, x, a]) => put(g, `who ${v} ${x}`, `${a} ${v} ${x}.`));
  const first = (g, s) => rows(s).forEach(([x, a]) => put(g, "who was the first " + x, `${a} was the first ${x}.`));
  const what = (g, s) => rows(s).forEach(([x, a]) => put(g, "what was the first " + x, `The first ${x} was ${a}.`));

  R(`
what is a noun|A noun names a person, place, thing or idea (e.g. teacher, Delhi, book, honesty).
what is a pronoun|A pronoun replaces a noun (e.g. he, she, it, they).
what is a verb|A verb expresses an action, event or state (e.g. run, is, become).
what is an adjective|An adjective describes a noun or pronoun (e.g. tall, red, beautiful).
what is an adverb|An adverb modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb (e.g. quickly, very, always).
what is a preposition|A preposition shows the relation of a noun or pronoun to another word (e.g. in, on, under).
what is a conjunction|A conjunction joins words, phrases or clauses (e.g. and, but, because).
what is an interjection|An interjection expresses sudden emotion (e.g. wow, alas, hurrah).
what is an article|The words a, an and the; "a" and "an" are indefinite, "the" is definite.
what is a determiner|A word placed before a noun to specify it (e.g. the, some, this, my).
how many parts of speech are there|Eight: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction and interjection.
how many tenses are there in english|Three main tenses (past, present, future), each with four aspects, giving twelve forms.
what are the three tenses|Past, present and future.
what is the simple present tense|It describes habits and general truths (e.g. She plays tennis).
what is the present continuous tense|It describes an action happening now (e.g. She is playing).
what is the present perfect tense|It links the past with the present (e.g. She has played).
what is the simple past tense|It describes a completed past action (e.g. She played).
what is the future simple tense|It describes a future action using will (e.g. She will play).
what is a subject|The person or thing that performs the action of the verb.
what is an object|The person or thing that receives the action of the verb.
what is a predicate|The part of a sentence that says something about the subject.
what is a clause|A group of words with a subject and a verb.
what is a phrase|A group of words without a subject-verb pair acting as one unit.
what is a simple sentence|A sentence with one independent clause.
what is a compound sentence|A sentence with two or more independent clauses joined by a conjunction.
what is a complex sentence|A sentence with one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.
what is an active voice|The subject performs the action (e.g. Ravi wrote the letter).
what is a passive voice|The subject receives the action (e.g. The letter was written by Ravi).
what is direct speech|The exact words of the speaker, in quotation marks.
what is indirect speech|Reporting what someone said without quoting exact words.
what is a synonym|A word with the same or nearly the same meaning as another word.
what is an antonym|A word with the opposite meaning of another word.
what is a homophone|A word that sounds like another but differs in meaning or spelling.
what is a homonym|A word with the same spelling or sound as another but a different meaning.
what is an idiom|A phrase whose meaning is not clear from its individual words.
what is a metaphor|A figure of speech saying one thing is another (e.g. Time is a thief).
what is a simile|A comparison using like or as (e.g. as brave as a lion).
what is personification|Giving human qualities to non-human things.
what is alliteration|Repetition of the same starting sound in nearby words.
what is onomatopoeia|A word that imitates a sound (e.g. buzz, splash).
what is hyperbole|Deliberate exaggeration for effect.
what is an oxymoron|Two contradictory words together (e.g. bittersweet).
what is a proverb|A short, well-known saying that states a general truth.
what is a prefix|A group of letters added at the start of a word to change its meaning.
what is a suffix|A group of letters added at the end of a word to change its meaning.
what is a gerund|A verb form ending in -ing that functions as a noun (e.g. Swimming is fun).
what is an infinitive|The base form of a verb, usually with to (e.g. to eat).
what is a participle|A verb form used as an adjective or in compound tenses (e.g. broken, running).
what is a countable noun|A noun that can be counted (e.g. book, apple).
what is an uncountable noun|A noun that cannot be counted (e.g. water, advice).
what is a proper noun|The name of a particular person, place or thing, starting with a capital letter.
what is a common noun|A general name for a class of people, places or things.
what is an abstract noun|A noun naming a quality, idea or feeling (e.g. honesty, joy).
what is a collective noun|A noun naming a group (e.g. team, herd).
what is a modal verb|A helping verb such as can, may, must, should or will.
what is an auxiliary verb|A helping verb such as be, do or have.
what is a transitive verb|A verb that takes a direct object.
what is an intransitive verb|A verb that does not take a direct object.
what is a comma used for|To separate items in a list, clauses and extra information.
what is a semicolon used for|To join two related independent clauses.
what is a colon used for|To introduce a list, explanation or quotation.
what is an apostrophe used for|To show possession or a contraction (e.g. Ravi's, don't).
what is a hyphen used for|To join words or parts of words (e.g. well-known).
what is the difference between its and it's|"Its" shows possession; "it's" means "it is" or "it has".
what is the difference between affect and effect|"Affect" is usually a verb (to influence); "effect" is usually a noun (a result).
what is the difference between fewer and less|Use "fewer" with countable nouns and "less" with uncountable ones.
what is the difference between who and whom|"Who" is the subject; "whom" is the object.
what is the difference between lie and lay|"Lie" means to recline; "lay" means to put something down.
what is the difference between then and than|"Then" refers to time; "than" is used for comparison.
what is the difference between there their and they're|"There" is a place, "their" shows possession, and "they're" means "they are".
what is the difference between your and you're|"Your" shows possession; "you're" means "you are".
what is the difference between accept and except|"Accept" means to receive; "except" means excluding.
what is the difference between principal and principle|"Principal" is a head or main; "principle" is a rule or belief.
what is the difference between stationary and stationery|"Stationary" means not moving; "stationery" means writing materials.
what is the difference between advice and advise|"Advice" is a noun; "advise" is a verb.
what is the difference between since and for|"Since" gives the starting point; "for" gives the duration.
what is the difference between little and a little|"Little" means hardly any; "a little" means some.
what is the difference between few and a few|"Few" means hardly any; "a few" means some.
`).forEach(([q, a]) => put("Grammar: Concepts", q, a));

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
// ENGLISH GRAMMAR RULES PACK
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
const rulesKeys = new Set();
(function rulesPack() {
  const G = {};
  const put = (g, k, a) => { k = k.toLowerCase().trim(); if (k in qaBank) return; qaBank[k] = a; rulesKeys.add(k); (G[g] = G[g] || []).push(k); };
  const R = s => s.trim().split("\n").map(r => r.trim()).filter(Boolean).map(r => r.split("|"));
  const gen = (g, rows, phr) => rows.forEach(r => phr.forEach(f => { const o = f(...r); if (o) put(g, o[0], o[1]); }));

  // ── 12 tenses
  gen("Rules: Tenses", R(`
simple present|S + V1 (add s/es for he/she/it)|habits, routines and general truths|always, usually, often, never, every day|She goes to school every day.|S + do/does + not + V1|Do/Does + S + V1?
present continuous|S + am/is/are + V-ing|actions happening now or temporary situations|now, at the moment, today, look!, listen!|He is reading a book now.|S + am/is/are + not + V-ing|Am/Is/Are + S + V-ing?
present perfect|S + has/have + V3|past actions with a result in the present|just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for|I have finished my work.|S + has/have + not + V3|Has/Have + S + V3?
present perfect continuous|S + has/have been + V-ing|actions that started in the past and are still continuing|since, for, how long, all day|She has been studying for two hours.|S + has/have + not + been + V-ing|Has/Have + S + been + V-ing?
simple past|S + V2|completed actions in the past|yesterday, ago, last week, in 2010|They played cricket yesterday.|S + did not + V1|Did + S + V1?
past continuous|S + was/were + V-ing|an action in progress at a point in the past|while, when, at 5 pm yesterday|I was watching TV when he came.|S + was/were + not + V-ing|Was/Were + S + V-ing?
past perfect|S + had + V3|the earlier of two past actions|before, after, by the time, already|The train had left before I reached.|S + had not + V3|Had + S + V3?
past perfect continuous|S + had been + V-ing|an action that continued up to a point in the past|since, for, how long (in the past)|He had been working for two hours when I came.|S + had not + been + V-ing|Had + S + been + V-ing?
simple future|S + will/shall + V1|predictions, promises and decisions made at the moment of speaking|tomorrow, next week, soon, tonight|I will call you tomorrow.|S + will not + V1|Will + S + V1?
future continuous|S + will be + V-ing|an action that will be in progress at a future time|this time tomorrow, at 5 pm tomorrow|I will be travelling this time tomorrow.|S + will not be + V-ing|Will + S + be + V-ing?
future perfect|S + will have + V3|an action that will be completed before a future time|by tomorrow, by next week, by then|She will have finished by 5 pm.|S + will not have + V3|Will + S + have + V3?
future perfect continuous|S + will have been + V-ing|how long an action will have continued by a future time|by next year, by then, for…by|By June I will have been working here for five years.|S + will not have been + V-ing|Will + S + have been + V-ing?
`), [
    (t, f, u, s, e, n, q) => [`${t} tense`, `${t[0].toUpperCase() + t.slice(1)} tense: formula ${f}. Used for ${u}. Example: ${e}`],
    (t, f, u, s, e, n, q) => [`what is ${t} tense`, `${t[0].toUpperCase() + t.slice(1)} tense: formula ${f}. Used for ${u}. Example: ${e}`],

    (t, f, u, s, e, n, q) => [`uses of ${t}`, `${t[0].toUpperCase() + t.slice(1)} is used for ${u}. Example: ${e}`],
    (t, f, u, s, e, n, q) => [`when to use ${t} tense`, `Use ${t} tense for ${u}. Example: ${e}`],
    (t, f, u, s, e, n, q) => [`${t} tense uses`, `Use ${t} tense for ${u}. Example: ${e}`],
    (t, f, u, s, e, n, q) => [`signal words of ${t}`, `Signal words of ${t}: ${s}.`],
    (t, f, u, s, e, n, q) => [`${t} tense signal words`, `Signal words of ${t}: ${s}.`],
    (t, f, u, s, e, n, q) => [`example of ${t} tense`, `Example of ${t}: ${e}`],
    (t, f, u, s, e, n, q) => [`${t} tense examples`, `Example of ${t}: ${e}`],
    (t, f, u, s, e, n, q) => [`negative of ${t} tense`, `Negative form of ${t}: ${n}.`],
    (t, f, u, s, e, n, q) => [`negative form of ${t}`, `Negative form of ${t}: ${n}.`],
    (t, f, u, s, e, n, q) => [`interrogative form of ${t}`, `Question form of ${t}: ${q}`],

  ]);
  put("Rules: Tenses", "how many tenses are there", "There are three main tenses (past, present, future), each with four forms (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous), giving 12 tenses.");
  put("Rules: Tenses", "list all 12 tenses", "Simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous forms of the present, past and future tenses.");
  put("Rules: Tenses", "what are the 12 tenses in english", "Simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous forms of the present, past and future tenses.");

  // ── Passive voice by tense
  gen("Rules: Voice", R(`
simple present|am/is/are + V3|The letter is written by him.
present continuous|am/is/are being + V3|The letter is being written by him.
present perfect|has/have been + V3|The letter has been written by him.
simple past|was/were + V3|The letter was written by him.
past continuous|was/were being + V3|The letter was being written by him.
past perfect|had been + V3|The letter had been written by him.
simple future|will be + V3|The letter will be written by him.
future perfect|will have been + V3|The letter will have been written by him.
modal verbs|modal + be + V3|The letter can be written by him.
`), [

  // ── Conditionals and question tags

zero conditional|If + present simple, present simple|facts and general truths|If you heat ice, it melts.

`), [

  // ── Rules (topic|text) with several phrasings
  const rules = R(`
a and an|Use "a" before a consonant sound and "an" before a vowel sound (a book, an apple, an hour, a university).
the definite article|Use "the" for specific or already mentioned things, unique things (the sun), superlatives, rivers, oceans, mountain ranges, and groups like the poor and the rich.
no article|Omit the article with plural or uncountable general nouns, meals, languages, sports and most proper names: Dogs bark; He plays cricket; We had lunch.
article before superlative|Use "the" before superlatives: She is the tallest girl.
article with unique things|Use "the" with unique things: the sun, the moon, the earth, the sky.
article with rivers seas and mountains|Use "the" with rivers, seas, oceans, deserts, gulfs and mountain ranges: the Ganga, the Pacific, the Himalayas.
article with musical instruments|Use "the" with musical instruments: She plays the guitar.
article with meals and sports|Do not use an article with meals, games and sports: We had lunch; He plays cricket.
article with languages|Do not use an article with languages: She speaks French.
article with professions|Use "a/an" to say what someone is: He is a doctor.
article with the poor and the rich|Use "the" with adjectives for groups: the poor, the rich, the young.
article with titles|Use "the" with unique titles: the Prime Minister, the President.
subject verb agreement|The verb must agree with its subject in number: a singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb.
subject verb agreement with and|Two subjects joined by "and" take a plural verb (Ram and Shyam are friends), unless they form one idea (Bread and butter is my breakfast).
subject verb agreement with or and nor|With "or", "nor", "either…or" and "neither…nor", the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it.
subject verb agreement with each and every|Each, every, either, neither, everyone, someone and nobody take singular verbs.
subject verb agreement with as well as|With "as well as", "along with", "together with" and "with", the verb agrees with the first subject.
subject verb agreement with collective nouns|A collective noun takes a singular verb when the group acts as one unit and a plural verb when its members act separately.
subject verb agreement with one of|"One of" is followed by a plural noun but a singular verb: One of my friends is a doctor.
subject verb agreement with a number of|"A number of" takes a plural verb; "the number of" takes a singular verb.
subject verb agreement with plural form nouns|News, mathematics, physics and measles are singular; scissors, trousers and spectacles are plural.
subject verb agreement with money time and distance|Expressions of money, time and distance take singular verbs: Ten kilometres is a long way.
subject verb agreement with many a|"Many a" takes a singular verb: Many a man has failed.
subject verb agreement with fractions|Fractions take a singular verb with uncountable nouns and a plural verb with plural nouns: Half of the cake is gone; half of the apples are gone.
subject verb agreement with relative pronouns|The verb after who, which or that agrees with its antecedent: He is one of those who work hard.
active voice|In the active voice the subject performs the action: Ravi wrote a letter.
passive voice|In the passive voice the subject receives the action; formula: object + be + V3 + by + subject: A letter was written by Ravi.
how to change active to passive|Move the object to the subject position, use the right form of "be" with V3, and add "by + agent": She sings a song → A song is sung by her.
passive voice of imperative sentences|Use "Let + object + be + V3": Open the door → Let the door be opened.
passive voice of questions|Invert the auxiliary: Who wrote this? → By whom was this written?
passive voice with two objects|Either object can become the subject: She gave me a book → I was given a book.
intransitive verbs and passive voice|Intransitive verbs have no object, so they cannot be made passive.
direct speech|Direct speech repeats the speaker's exact words inside quotation marks: He said, "I am tired."
indirect speech|Indirect speech reports what was said without quoting: He said that he was tired.
direct to indirect speech|Remove the quotation marks, add "that", change the pronouns, tense and time/place words, and keep the reporting verb.
indirect speech when the reporting verb is present|If the reporting verb is in the present or future tense, the tense of the reported speech does not change.
indirect speech of universal truth|If the reported speech is a universal truth, its tense does not change: He said that the sun rises in the east.
indirect speech of questions|Use "asked" and "if/whether" for yes/no questions or the same wh-word for others, in statement order: She asked, "Where do you live?" → She asked where I lived.
indirect speech of commands|Use "told/ordered/requested" with a to-infinitive: He said, "Open the door" → He told me to open the door.
indirect speech of exclamations|Use "exclaimed with joy/sorrow/surprise that…": He said, "Hurrah! We won" → He exclaimed with joy that they had won.
indirect speech of wishes|Use "wished/prayed that…": He said, "May you succeed" → He wished that I might succeed.
pronoun changes in indirect speech|First person pronouns change according to the subject of the reporting verb, second person according to its object, and third person pronouns stay the same.
unless|"Unless" means "if not": Unless you hurry, you will be late.
wish sentences|Use the past simple for present wishes (I wish I were taller) and the past perfect for past regrets (I wish I had studied).
subjunctive mood|Use "were" for all subjects in unreal conditions, and the base verb after verbs like suggest, demand and insist: I suggest that he go.
can|"Can" expresses ability, permission or possibility: She can swim.
could|"Could" is the past of can and expresses polite requests and possibility: Could you help me?
may|"May" expresses permission, possibility and wishes: May I come in?
might|"Might" expresses weak possibility: It might rain.
must|"Must" expresses obligation, strong necessity or logical certainty: You must obey the law.
should|"Should" expresses advice or duty: You should exercise daily.
ought to|"Ought to" expresses moral duty and advice: You ought to respect elders.
will and would|"Will" shows future, willingness or promises; "would" shows polite requests, past habits or unreal situations.
shall|"Shall" is used with I and we for offers, suggestions and future: Shall we go?
used to|"Used to" + V1 describes past habits or states: He used to smoke.
need and dare|"Need" and "dare" act as modals in negatives and questions: You needn't worry; How dare you?
had better|"Had better" + V1 gives strong advice: You had better leave now.
modal verbs|Modal verbs are followed by the base form of the verb, have no -s in the third person, and form questions by inversion.
prepositions of time in on at|Use "at" for exact times (at 5 pm), "on" for days and dates (on Monday), and "in" for months, years, seasons and long periods (in May, in 2020).
prepositions of place in on at|Use "in" for enclosed spaces and cities, "on" for surfaces, and "at" for specific points: in the room, on the table, at the door.
since and for|Use "since" with a point in time and "for" with a period: since 2010, for ten years.
between and among|Use "between" for two and "among" for more than two.
beside and besides|"Beside" means next to; "besides" means in addition to.
in and into|"In" shows position; "into" shows movement: He is in the room; he went into the room.
by and with|Use "by" for the doer and "with" for the instrument: written by him with a pen.
till and until|Both mean up to a time; "until" is more formal.
during and for|"During" says when something happens; "for" says how long.
on time and in time|"On time" means punctual; "in time" means early enough.
coordinating conjunctions|The coordinating conjunctions are for, and, nor, but, or, yet and so (FANBOYS).
subordinating conjunctions|Subordinating conjunctions such as although, because, if, when, while and unless introduce dependent clauses.
correlative conjunctions|Correlative conjunctions come in pairs: either…or, neither…nor, both…and, not only…but also, whether…or.
although and but|Do not use "although" and "but" together in one sentence: Although he was tired, he worked.
because and so|Do not use "because" and "so" together in one sentence.
hardly scarcely and no sooner|"Hardly" and "scarcely" are followed by "when" and "no sooner" by "than": No sooner had he come than it rained.
not only but also|The structures after "not only" and "but also" must be parallel.
neither nor|"Neither…nor" takes a verb that agrees with the nearer subject.
so that and such that|Use "so that" for purpose and "so…that" or "such…that" for result.
full stop|Use a full stop at the end of a statement or command.
comma|Use commas to separate items in a list, after introductory phrases, before conjunctions joining clauses, and around extra information.
comma splice|A comma splice joins two independent clauses with only a comma; fix it with a full stop, semicolon or conjunction.
semicolon|Use a semicolon to join two closely related independent clauses.
colon|Use a colon to introduce a list, an explanation or a quotation.
apostrophe|Use an apostrophe for contractions (don't) and possession (Ravi's book), never for plurals.
possessive nouns|Add 's to singular nouns (boy's) and only an apostrophe after plural nouns ending in s (boys').
quotation marks|Use quotation marks around direct speech and quotations, with punctuation inside them.
question mark|Use a question mark after a direct question, not after an indirect question.
exclamation mark|Use an exclamation mark after strong feelings or commands.
hyphen|Use a hyphen to join compound adjectives before a noun (a well-known actor) and in numbers like twenty-one.
dash|Use a dash for a sudden break or to add emphasis.
brackets|Use brackets to add extra information that is not essential.
ellipsis|Three dots show omitted words or a trailing thought.
capital letters|Capitalise the first word of a sentence, the pronoun I, proper nouns, days, months, titles and the main words in headings.
order of adjectives|Adjectives follow the order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose (a lovely small old round red Italian leather bag).
comparative degree|Use -er for one-syllable adjectives and "more" for most longer ones; use "than" after a comparative.
superlative degree|Use -est or "most" with "the": the tallest, the most beautiful.
double comparative|Never use two comparatives together: "more better" is wrong; say "better".
as as comparison|Use "as…as" for equality and "not so/as…as" for inequality: She is as tall as him.
elder and older|"Elder" is used only for family members and without "than"; "older" can be used with "than".
adjective and adverb|An adjective describes a noun; an adverb describes a verb, adjective or adverb: She is quick; she runs quickly.
position of adverbs of frequency|Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb but after "be": He always works; he is always late.
too and enough|"Too" means more than needed and comes before an adjective; "enough" comes after an adjective: too hot; hot enough.
very and much|"Very" modifies adjectives and adverbs; "much" modifies comparatives and verbs: very good, much better.
good and well|"Good" is an adjective; "well" is usually an adverb: She sings well.
personal pronoun cases|Personal pronouns have subject (I, he), object (me, him) and possessive (my, mine) forms.
pronoun after a preposition|Use the object case after prepositions: between you and me.
pronoun after than and as|After "than" and "as" use the subject case if a verb is understood: She is taller than I (am).
reflexive pronouns|Reflexive pronouns end in -self or -selves and refer back to the subject: He hurt himself.
relative pronouns|Who is for persons, which for things and animals, whose for possession, and that for both.
who and whom|Use "who" as the subject and "whom" as the object: The man whom I met.
pronoun agreement|A pronoun must agree with its antecedent in number, gender and person.
order of pronouns|For good things use 2nd, 3rd, 1st person (You, he and I); for faults or blame use 1st, 2nd, 3rd (I, you and he).
each other and one another|"Each other" is for two; "one another" is for more than two.
possessive adjectives and pronouns|Possessive adjectives (my, your) come before nouns; possessive pronouns (mine, yours) stand alone.
plural rules|Add -s to most nouns, -es to nouns ending in s, x, z, ch, sh, change consonant + y to -ies, and f/fe to -ves for many words.
nouns ending in o|Many nouns ending in o take -es (potatoes), but music and foreign words take -s (pianos, photos).
compound noun plurals|In compound nouns, the main noun takes the plural: brothers-in-law.
much and many|Use "many" and "few" with countable nouns; "much" and "little" with uncountable nouns.
some and any|Use "some" in positive sentences and offers; use "any" in negatives and questions.
a few and few|"A few" means some; "few" means hardly any. The same applies to "a little" and "little".
gerund|A gerund is the -ing form used as a noun: Swimming is good exercise.
gerund after prepositions|A preposition is followed by a gerund: He is fond of reading.
verbs followed by gerund|Verbs like enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, practise and suggest are followed by a gerund.
verbs followed by infinitive|Verbs like want, hope, decide, plan, promise and refuse are followed by to + V1.
bare infinitive|Use the infinitive without "to" after modals and after let, make, help and see/hear verbs.
stop with gerund and infinitive|"Stop doing" means to quit; "stop to do" means to pause in order to do something.
participle|A participle is a verb form used as an adjective: a broken glass, a running horse.
dangling modifier|A dangling modifier does not clearly refer to the word it modifies; keep modifiers next to the word they describe.
parallel structure|Items in a series must have the same grammatical form: She likes reading, writing and singing.
sentence fragment|A fragment lacks a subject or a complete verb and cannot stand alone.
run-on sentence|A run-on sentence joins independent clauses without proper punctuation or conjunctions.
types of sentences by function|Declarative (statement), interrogative (question), imperative (command), exclamatory (feeling) and optative (wish).
types of sentences by structure|Simple, compound, complex and compound-complex.
phrase and clause|A phrase has no subject-verb pair; a clause has both.
types of clauses|Independent clauses stand alone; dependent clauses include noun, adjective and adverb clauses.
types of nouns|Common, proper, collective, material and abstract nouns, and countable and uncountable nouns.
types of pronouns|Personal, possessive, reflexive, demonstrative, interrogative, relative, indefinite and reciprocal pronouns.
types of adjectives|Descriptive, quantitative, numeral, demonstrative, interrogative and possessive adjectives.
types of adverbs|Adverbs of manner, place, time, frequency, degree and reason.
types of verbs|Action verbs, linking verbs, auxiliary verbs, modal verbs, transitive and intransitive verbs.
i before e spelling rule|Write "i before e except after c": believe, receive.
silent e spelling rule|Drop the silent e before a suffix beginning with a vowel: make → making.
doubling consonant spelling rule|Double the final consonant of one-syllable consonant-vowel-consonant words before a vowel suffix: run → running.
y to i spelling rule|Change y to i before adding a suffix when a consonant precedes y: happy → happiness.
full spelling rule|"Full" loses one l when added to a word: beautiful, careful.
third person singular spelling|Add -s to most verbs, -es to verbs ending in s, sh, ch, x, z, o, and change consonant + y to -ies.
ing spelling rules|Drop the e (make → making), double the final consonant in CVC words (run → running) and change ie to y (lie → lying).
ed spelling rules|Add -ed (walked); add -d to words ending in e (loved); change y to ied (studied); double the final consonant (stopped).
too to structure|"Too…to" has a negative meaning: He is too weak to walk means He is so weak that he cannot walk.
so that structure|"So…that" shows result: She was so tired that she slept.
such that structure|Use "such a/an + adjective + noun + that": It was such a hot day that we stayed in.
there is and there are|Use "there is" with singular and uncountable nouns and "there are" with plural nouns.
make and do|"Make" is for creating or producing (make a cake); "do" is for actions and tasks (do homework).
say and tell|"Say" does not need a person as object; "tell" does: He told me; he said hello.
lie and lay|"Lie" is intransitive (lie–lay–lain); "lay" is transitive (lay–laid–laid).
rise and raise|"Rise" has no object; "raise" takes an object.
bring and take|"Bring" means toward the speaker; "take" means away from the speaker.
borrow and lend|"Borrow" means to receive; "lend" means to give temporarily.
whose and who's|"Who's" is "who is"; "whose" shows possession.
double negatives|Two negatives make a positive; avoid them: "I don't know nothing" is wrong.
redundancy|Avoid saying the same thing twice, such as "return back" or "repeat again".
as and like|Use "like" with nouns to compare; use "as" with clauses.
since as and because|"Since" and "as" give known reasons; "because" gives the main reason.
whether and if|Use "whether" for alternatives: I don't know whether he will come or not.
sequence of tenses|If the main clause is in the past tense, the subordinate clause is usually also in a past form.
past perfect rule|When two past actions occur, use the past perfect for the earlier one.
present perfect and simple past|Use the present perfect without a definite past time; use the simple past with finished time words (yesterday, ago).
future in time clauses|After when, if, as soon as, before and after, use the present simple for future meaning.
sentence word order|English sentences follow subject-verb-object order; adverbs of time often come at the end.
question formation|Questions are formed by inverting the auxiliary and the subject: Do you like tea?
imperative sentence|An imperative uses the base verb with an understood "you": Close the door.
exclamatory sentence|Exclamations often start with "what" or "how": What a beautiful day!
optative sentence|An optative sentence expresses a wish or prayer: May you live long!
`);
  gen("Rules: Grammar", rules, [
    (t, r) => [`rule for ${t}`, r],
    (t, r) => [`rules of ${t}`, r],
    (t, r) => [`${t} rule`, r],
    (t, r) => [`${t} rules`, r],
    (t, r) => [`explain ${t}`, r],
    (t, r) => [`how to use ${t}`, r],
    (t, r) => [`${t} with examples`, r],
    (t, r) => [`what is the rule of ${t}`, r],
    (t, r) => [`${t} grammar`, r],
    (t, r) => [`${t} grammar rule`, r],
  ]);

  // ── Figures of speech
  gen("Rules: Figures of Speech", R(`
simile|a comparison using like or as|He is as brave as a lion.
metaphor|a direct comparison without like or as|Time is a thief.
personification|giving human qualities to non-human things|The wind whispered through the trees.
hyperbole|deliberate exaggeration for effect|I have told you a million times.
oxymoron|two contradictory words together|bittersweet
alliteration|repetition of the same starting sound in nearby words|Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.
onomatopoeia|a word that imitates a sound|buzz, splash
irony|saying the opposite of what is meant|"What lovely weather!" said during a storm.
pun|a play on words with double meaning|I used to be a banker, but I lost interest.
euphemism|a mild word used for something unpleasant|"passed away" for "died"
antithesis|contrast of opposite ideas in balanced phrases|To err is human, to forgive divine.
apostrophe|addressing an absent person or thing directly|O Death, where is thy sting?
synecdoche|a part stands for the whole|"All hands on deck" for sailors
metonymy|naming something by something closely linked to it|"The crown" for the monarchy
litotes|understatement by denying the opposite|He is not a bad singer.
climax|arranging ideas in increasing order of importance|I came, I saw, I conquered.
anticlimax|a sudden drop from the important to the trivial|She lost her husband, her home and her umbrella.
paradox|a statement that seems contradictory but contains truth|The child is the father of the man.
epigram|a short witty saying|The only way to get rid of temptation is to yield to it.
understatement|saying less than is meant|"It's a bit chilly" in a blizzard.
transferred epithet|an adjective shifted from the person to a related noun|a sleepless night
anaphora|repetition of a word at the start of successive lines|We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds.
assonance|repetition of vowel sounds in nearby words|The rain in Spain stays mainly in the plain.
consonance|repetition of consonant sounds in nearby words|pitter-patter
pathetic fallacy|giving human emotions to nature|The angry sea roared.
allusion|an indirect reference to a person, place or event|He is a Romeo.
`), [
    (n, d, e) => [`what is ${n}`, `${n[0].toUpperCase() + n.slice(1)} is ${d}. Example: ${e}`],
    (n, d, e) => [`define ${n}`, `${n[0].toUpperCase() + n.slice(1)} is ${d}. Example: ${e}`],
    (n, d, e) => [`${n} definition`, `${n[0].toUpperCase() + n.slice(1)} is ${d}.`],
    (n, d, e) => [`${n} example`, `Example of ${n}: ${e}`],
    (n, d, e) => [`figure of speech ${n}`, `${n[0].toUpperCase() + n.slice(1)} is ${d}. Example: ${e}`],

    (n, d, e) => [`${n} in english grammar`, `${n[0].toUpperCase() + n.slice(1)} is ${d}. Example: ${e}`],
  ]);

  Object.keys(G).forEach(gr => { const a = G[gr], s = Math.max(1, Math.floor(a.length / 100)); chapterKeys["★ " + gr] = a.filter((_, i) => i % s === 0).slice(0, 100); });
  window.rulesCount = rulesKeys.size;
})();

// GRAMMAR PRACTICE: voice, tense and sentence conversion (generated)
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
const pracKeys = new Set();
(function pracPack() {
  const G = {};
  const put = (g, k, a) => { k = k.toLowerCase().trim(); if (k in qaBank) return; qaBank[k] = a; pracKeys.add(k); (G[g] = G[g] || []).push(k); };
  const cap = s => s[0].toUpperCase() + s.slice(1);
  const V = `write|writes|wrote|written|writing|a letter
read|reads|read|read|reading|the book
eat|eats|ate|eaten|eating|an apple
sing|sings|sang|sung|singing|a song
paint|paints|painted|painted|painting|a picture
break|breaks|broke|broken|breaking|the window
drive|drives|drove|driven|driving|the car
open|opens|opened|opened|opening|the door
see|sees|saw|seen|seeing|the film
build|builds|built|built|building|a house
cook|cooks|cooked|cooked|cooking|the meal
play|plays|played|played|playing|the game
bake|bakes|baked|baked|baking|a cake
fix|fixes|fixed|fixed|fixing|the machine
clean|cleans|cleaned|cleaned|cleaning|the room
catch|catches|caught|caught|catching|the ball
send|sends|sent|sent|sending|a message
buy|buys|bought|bought|buying|a gift
take|takes|took|taken|taking|the photo
teach|teaches|taught|taught|teaching|the lesson
close|closes|closed|closed|closing|the shop
draw|draws|drew|drawn|drawing|a map
solve|solves|solved|solved|solving|the problem
wash|washes|washed|washed|washing|the shirt
carry|carries|carried|carried|carrying|the bag`.split("\n").map(r => r.split("|"));
  const S = [["Ravi", "Ravi"], ["She", "her"], ["He", "him"], ["The teacher", "the teacher"], ["My mother", "my mother"]];
  const mid = s => (s === "Ravi" ? s : s[0].toLowerCase() + s.slice(1));
  const T = [
    ["simple present", "is"], ["present continuous", "is being"], ["present perfect", "has been"], ["simple past", "was"],
    ["past continuous", "was being"], ["past perfect", "had been"], ["simple future", "will be"], ["future perfect", "will have been"],
  ];

  V.forEach(([v1, vs, v2, v3, ving, o]) => S.forEach(([s, ag]) => {
    const m = mid(s);
    const act = [`${s} ${vs} ${o}.`, `${s} is ${ving} ${o}.`, `${s} has ${v3} ${o}.`, `${s} ${v2} ${o}.`, `${s} was ${ving} ${o}.`, `${s} had ${v3} ${o}.`, `${s} will ${v1} ${o}.`, `${s} will have ${v3} ${o}.`];
    act.forEach((a, i) => {
      const [tn, aux] = T[i];
      const p = `${cap(o)} ${aux} ${v3} by ${ag}.`;
      put("Practice: Active to Passive", `change into passive voice: ${a}`, `${p}`);
      put("Practice: Active to Passive", `passive voice of: ${a}`, `${p} (${tn})`);
      put("Practice: Active to Passive", `convert to passive: ${a}`, `${p}`);
      put("Practice: Passive to Active", `change into active voice: ${p}`, `${a}`);
      put("Practice: Passive to Active", `active voice of: ${p}`, `${a} (${tn})`);
      put("Practice: Voice and Tense", `identify the voice: ${a}`, `Active voice.`);
      put("Practice: Voice and Tense", `identify the voice: ${p}`, `Passive voice.`);
      put("Practice: Voice and Tense", `identify the tense: ${a}`, `${cap(tn)} tense.`);
    });
    // tense conversions from the simple present sentence
    const conv = [
      ["past tense", act[3]], ["simple past", act[3]], ["future tense", act[6]], ["simple future", act[6]],
      ["present continuous", act[1]], ["present perfect", act[2]], ["past continuous", act[4]], ["past perfect", act[5]], ["future perfect", act[7]],
    ];
    conv.forEach(([tn, a]) => {
      put("Practice: Tense Conversion", `change into ${tn}: ${act[0]}`, a);
      put("Practice: Tense Conversion", `convert to ${tn}: ${act[0]}`, a);
    });
    put("Practice: Negative and Interrogative", `make negative: ${act[0]}`, `${s} does not ${v1} ${o}.`);
    put("Practice: Negative and Interrogative", `make interrogative: ${act[0]}`, `Does ${m} ${v1} ${o}?`);
    put("Practice: Negative and Interrogative", `make negative: ${act[3]}`, `${s} did not ${v1} ${o}.`);
    put("Practice: Negative and Interrogative", `make interrogative: ${act[3]}`, `Did ${m} ${v1} ${o}?`);
    put("Practice: Negative and Interrogative", `change into negative: ${act[0]}`, `${s} does not ${v1} ${o}.`);
    put("Practice: Negative and Interrogative", `change into interrogative: ${act[0]}`, `Does ${m} ${v1} ${o}?`);
    put("Practice: Negative and Interrogative", `change into negative: ${act[6]}`, `${s} will not ${v1} ${o}.`);
    put("Practice: Negative and Interrogative", `change into interrogative: ${act[6]}`, `Will ${m} ${v1} ${o}?`);
  }));

  Object.keys(G).forEach(gr => { const a = G[gr], st = Math.max(1, Math.floor(a.length / 100)); chapterKeys["★ " + gr] = a.filter((_, i) => i % st === 0).slice(0, 100); });
  window.pracCount = pracKeys.size;
})();

second|salaries of the President, Governors, judges and other officials
third|forms of oaths and affirmations
fourth|allocation of Rajya Sabha seats
fifth|administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes
sixth|administration of tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram
seventh|the Union, State and Concurrent Lists
eighth|the recognised languages
ninth|land reform and other laws shielded from judicial review
tenth|the anti-defection law
eleventh|the powers of Panchayats
twelfth|the powers of municipalities
`), [
    (n, t) => [`${n} schedule of the indian constitution`, `The ${n} Schedule deals with ${t}.`],
    (n, t) => [`what is in the ${n} schedule`, `The ${n} Schedule deals with ${t}.`],
    (n, t) => [`${n} schedule`, `The ${n} Schedule deals with ${t}.`],
    (n, t) => [`what does the ${n} schedule deal with`, `The ${n} Schedule deals with ${t}.`],
    (n, t) => [`${n} schedule contains`, `The ${n} Schedule deals with ${t}.`],
  ]);

  // ── Maths helpers
  const rom = n => { const m = [[1000, "M"], [900, "CM"], [500, "D"], [400, "CD"], [100, "C"], [90, "XC"], [50, "L"], [40, "XL"], [10, "X"], [9, "IX"], [5, "V"], [4, "IV"], [1, "I"]]; let s = ""; m.forEach(([v, r]) => { while (n >= v) { s += r; n -= v; } }); return s; };
  const ones = "zero one two three four five six seven eight nine ten eleven twelve thirteen fourteen fifteen sixteen seventeen eighteen nineteen".split(" ");
  const tens = "- - twenty thirty forty fifty sixty seventy eighty ninety".split(" ");
  const words = n => n < 20 ? ones[n] : n < 100 ? tens[Math.floor(n / 10)] + (n % 10 ? "-" + ones[n % 10] : "") : n < 1000 ? ones[Math.floor(n / 100)] + " hundred" + (n % 100 ? " and " + words(n % 100) : "") : "one thousand";
  const isPrime = n => { if (n < 2) return false; for (let i = 2; i * i <= n; i++) if (n % i === 0) return false; return true; };
  const M = "GK2: Maths and Numbers";
  for (let n = 1; n <= 30; n++) {
    const r = rom(n);
    [`roman numeral of ${n}`, `${n} in roman numerals`, `write ${n} in roman numerals`, `roman number for ${n}`].forEach(k => put(M, k, `${n} in Roman numerals is ${r}.`));
    [`${r} in numbers`, `what is ${r} in numbers`, `roman numeral ${r} value`, `value of ${r}`, `convert ${r} to number`].forEach(k => put(M, k, `${r} = ${n}.`));
  }
  for (let n = 1; n <= 30; n++) {
    const w = words(n);
    [`write ${n} in words`, `${n} in words`, `how do you spell ${n} in words`].forEach(k => put(M, k, `${n} in words is ${w}.`));
  }
  for (let n = 1; n <= 15; n++) {
    [`square of ${n}`, `what is the square of ${n}`, `${n} squared`].forEach(k => put(M, k, `The square of ${n} is ${n * n}.`));
    [`square root of ${n * n}`, `what is the square root of ${n * n}`, `root of ${n * n}`].forEach(k => put(M, k, `The square root of ${n * n} is ${n}.`));
  }
  for (let n = 1; n <= 8; n++) {
    [`cube of ${n}`, `what is the cube of ${n}`, `${n} cubed`].forEach(k => put(M, k, `The cube of ${n} is ${n ** 3}.`));
    [`cube root of ${n ** 3}`, `what is the cube root of ${n ** 3}`].forEach(k => put(M, k, `The cube root of ${n ** 3} is ${n}.`));
  }
  for (let n = 2; n <= 50; n++) {
    const p = isPrime(n);
    [`is ${n} a prime number`, `is ${n} prime`].forEach(k => put(M, k, p ? `Yes, ${n} is a prime number.` : `No, ${n} is not prime (divisible by ${[...Array(n).keys()].slice(2).find(i => n % i === 0)}).`));
  }
  for (let a = 2; a <= 10; a++) for (let b = 1; b <= 5; b++) {
    [`${a} x ${b}`, `${a} times ${b}`, `${a} multiplied by ${b}`, `what is ${a} multiplied by ${b}`].forEach(k => put(M, k, `${a} × ${b} = ${a * b}.`));
  }

  Object.keys(G).forEach(gr => { const a = G[gr], s = Math.max(1, Math.floor(a.length / 100)); chapterKeys["★ " + gr] = a.filter((_, i) => i % s === 0).slice(0, 100); });
  window.gk2Count = gk2Keys.size;
})();
